variants.wording: What is the difference between IEnumerable and IQueryable?

sections.content: IEnumerable<T> provides synchronous enumeration. Operators applied as LINQ-to-Objects run .NET delegates while items are enumerated. IQueryable<T> also supports enumeration but carries an expression tree and query provider; EF Core translates supported expressions into database operations.

For an EF query, compose Where, Select, OrderBy and Take before materializing with ToListAsync so the database filters and returns only required columns. Calling ToList early loads results into memory; AsEnumerable changes subsequent operator binding to LINQ-to-Objects without itself necessarily materializing. Deferred execution means enumerating a query twice can run it twice.

Inspect generated SQL, recognize unsupported translations, and avoid arbitrary IQueryable exposure outside the data-access boundary. Neither interface guarantees speed: the provider, expression and data volume determine performance. An in-memory collection exposed as IQueryable does not become a remote database query.

variants.wording: 3.Explain one example with Dictionary and HashTable/Hashmaps.

sections.content: Dictionary<TKey,TValue> is a generic hash-based map. It provides compile-time key/value types and expected constant-time lookup and insertion when hashing is well distributed. Hashtable stores object keys and values, requiring casts and boxing for value types; use it mainly for legacy compatibility.

For counting words, the word is the key and the count is the value. Equality and the hash code must agree, and a key's equality-relevant state must remain stable while stored. Dictionary is not safe for concurrent writers; use synchronization or ConcurrentDictionary, considering atomic compound operations.

variants.wording: 𝟭/ 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰: Belongs to the type itself rather than a specific instance.

sections.content: static means a member belongs to the type rather than an object instance. A static method has no this reference, and a static class cannot be instantiated. Static state is shared within its runtime type context; separate closed generic types have separate static fields.

Good uses include pure calculation helpers and constants associated with a type. Mutable static collections require synchronization and often become memory-retention roots. Static does not mean thread-safe and does not create a singleton managed by the dependency injection container.

In a web service, avoid storing current user, tenant, DbContext, or request data in static fields. Shared caches should have explicit bounds and invalidation. Prefer injectable services when behavior needs configuration, substitution, or lifecycle management.

variants.wording: 𝟮/ 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁: Defines a constant value known at compile time.

sections.content: const declares a value computable at compile time, such as a numeric literal or string. Constants are implicitly static and cannot be reassigned. A consumer can embed a public constant's value into its compiled assembly.

This embedding matters for versioned libraries: changing the provider's constant does not necessarily change already-compiled consumers. Use static readonly for a value that can change between library versions or must be initialized at runtime, and configuration for operational values such as endpoints or retry limits.

For example, const int DaysPerWeek = 7 expresses an invariant, while a service URL should not be a constant baked into multiple deployments. const reference values are restricted; it is not a mechanism for making arbitrary objects immutable.

variants.wording: 𝟯/ 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆: Can only be assigned at declaration or in the constructor.

sections.content: A readonly instance field can be assigned in its declaration or an instance constructor of the declaring type. A static readonly field can be assigned at declaration or in its static constructor. It supports runtime initialization, unlike const.

Readonly prevents reassigning the field after initialization; it does not freeze the referenced object. A readonly List<int> can still have items added. Use immutable collections or carefully controlled APIs if the entire value must remain immutable.

Readonly structs and readonly members provide additional language guarantees around value-type mutation, but those are different from a readonly field. In interviews, show this distinction with a field whose list contents can change while its reference cannot.

variants.wording: 𝟱/ 𝘆𝗶𝗲𝗹𝗱: Simplifies iterators by returning values as they are requested.

sections.content: yield return produces the next element of an iterator and suspends it until the caller requests another. The compiler generates iterator state, so locals survive across MoveNext calls. yield break ends iteration.

This supports streaming transformations without building an intermediate list. The iterator body usually starts when enumeration begins, not when the method returning IEnumerable is called. Exceptions and resource access therefore also occur during enumeration; repeated enumeration repeats the work.

Use using or try/finally for resources so disposal happens when enumeration finishes or the enumerator is disposed. For asynchronously produced data, an async iterator returns IAsyncEnumerable<T> and uses await foreach. Lazy iteration is not automatically thread-safe or a substitute for pagination.

variants.wording: 𝟲/ 𝗿𝗲𝗳: Passes a variable by reference so the method can modify it.
𝟳/ 𝗼𝘂𝘁: Passes by reference, but the called method must assign a value.

sections.content: ref aliases caller storage and allows reading and writing; the caller must initialize the variable. out also aliases storage but requires the callee to assign it on every normal return path, so the caller need not initialize it. in supplies a readonly reference useful for avoiding copies of sufficiently large value types.

Passing a reference-type variable normally already permits mutating the object it points to. ref is needed when the method must replace the caller's variable itself. For in parameters, calling non-readonly struct members can introduce defensive copies, so performance must be measured.

Use TryParse-style out parameters for conventional success-plus-result APIs; tuples or result objects are often clearer for multiple results. Reference parameters impose language restrictions, including restrictions for async methods, so they should not be used as a general substitute for ordinary return values.
Example

variants.wording: 𝟴/ 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗺𝘀: Allows a method to accept a variable number of arguments.

sections.content: params lets callers supply zero or more arguments to one final parameter, traditionally an array such as params string[] values. A caller may also pass an existing compatible array, avoiding construction of another argument array in that form.

The method still receives a collection and must validate its contents. Overloads can become ambiguous, and hot paths can incur allocation costs when the compiler creates an argument collection. Newer C# versions support additional params collection forms, so specify the project's language version when using them.
Use params for ergonomic helpers such as formatting or combining tags. Prefer an explicit collection for large batches and stable API contracts where allocation and ownership matter.

variants.wording: 𝟵/ 𝗶𝘀 / 𝗮𝘀: Used for type checking and safe type conversion.

sections.content: is checks runtime compatibility and supports pattern matching: if (value is Customer customer) both tests and binds a typed variable. A failed test is false; null does not match a non-null type pattern.

as performs an allowed reference or nullable conversion and returns null when it fails. It does not perform arbitrary numeric parsing or user-defined conversions. An explicit cast throws for an invalid reference conversion, which is appropriate if failure violates an invariant.

Prefer pattern matching when you immediately use the converted value. Avoid as followed by unchecked member access because that replaces an understandable type mismatch with a NullReferenceException. Use domain polymorphism instead of growing type-switch chains when behavior naturally belongs to the type.

variants.wording: 𝟭𝟭/ 𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲: Accesses members or constructors of the base class.

sections.content: base accesses an accessible member of the immediate base class or selects a base constructor through a constructor initializer. It is useful when an override extends rather than completely replaces base behavior.

A derived constructor must establish the base portion of the object before its own body runs. A base call is statically targeted to base implementation; it is not another virtual dispatch to the same override.

Use inheritance where substitutability is true. A derived class that must constantly bypass base rules is a sign composition would be clearer. Avoid virtual calls from constructors because derived state may not yet be initialized.

variants.wording: 𝟭𝟮/ 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀: Refers to the current instance.

sections.content: this refers to the current instance and distinguishes fields from identically named parameters. this(...) delegates from one constructor to another constructor on the same type, helping centralize initialization.
It is unavailable in static methods because no current object exists. In the traditional extension-method syntax, this on the first parameter marks the receiver; that method is still a static method.

Passing this into callbacks during construction can expose a partially initialized object. Locking this makes synchronization publicly reachable, so a private lock object is safer. Use this where it improves clarity rather than treating it as a required prefix everywhere.

variants.wording: 𝟭𝟯/ 𝗻𝗲𝘄: Creates an object or hides an inherited member.

sections.content: new constructs an instance or array, for example new Customer(). It also serves as an explicit declaration that a member hides an inherited member with the same name. These meanings should not be confused.

With member hiding, a call through a base-typed reference chooses the base member, while a derived-typed reference can choose the hidden member. override instead participates in virtual dispatch and chooses the runtime implementation even through a base reference.

Generic constraints can also use new() to require a public parameterless constructor. For normal service replacement, interfaces and virtual overrides are clearer than hiding; hiding is mainly for deliberate API compatibility or special hierarchy requirements.

variants.wording: 𝟭𝟰/ 𝗮𝗯𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁: Defines classes or members intended for implementation by derived types.
102. When would you use an Abstract Class vs Interface? Explain with a real-time example.

sections.content: An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly. It can define constructors, shared state, implemented members and abstract members. A class can inherit only one base class. An interface represents a capability contract; a type can implement multiple interfaces.

Modern C# interfaces may contain default implementations and certain static members, so 'interfaces never contain implementations' is outdated. They still do not provide the ordinary per-instance field and constructor model of a base class.

For example, IPaymentGateway separates checkout from provider details. An abstract report exporter can share common validation and require a Render method. Prefer an interface when implementations should be independent; prefer a base class when shared invariants and lifecycle truly belong to one family. Do not invent a base class just to reuse two utility methods.

variants.wording: 𝟭𝟱/ 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗱: Prevents a class from being inherited.

sections.content: A sealed class cannot be subclassed. A sealed override prevents further overriding of that member while allowing the containing class itself to remain inheritable.

Seal a type when subclassing could violate its invariants or when no inheritance extension contract is intended. It can also enable runtime optimizations, but design intent should lead the decision rather than speculative speed.

Sealing does not make instances immutable, thread-safe or unmockable through interfaces. Tests can substitute an injected interface. If callers need customization, provide composition points or explicit strategies rather than exposing fragile inheritance behavior.

variants.wording: 𝟭𝟲/ 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗿𝗶𝗱𝗲: Provides a new implementation of an inherited virtual member.
101. What is the difference between Method Overriding and Method Hiding?

sections.content: override supplies a new implementation of an inherited virtual or abstract member. Calls use the runtime object's implementation even when the reference is typed as the base class. new hides a member and lookup depends on the reference's compile-time type.

For example, Base b = new Derived(); b.Describe() invokes Derived.Describe when it overrides a virtual method, but invokes Base.Describe when Derived merely hides it. Overloading is different again: methods share a name but differ in parameters, with selection mostly at compile time.

Use overriding to preserve substitutability and the base method's contract. A derived method should not unexpectedly strengthen preconditions or remove promised behavior. Hiding should be explicit and rare because different callers can observe surprising results.

variants.wording: 𝟭𝟳/ 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹: Splits a type definition across multiple files.

sections.content: partial allows one type's declarations to be split across source files; the compiler merges them into one type. It is common for generated code and human-maintained code to coexist without editing generated files.

All pieces must describe the same type in compatible namespaces and assemblies, with compatible modifiers. There is no runtime delegation between the files and no performance improvement from splitting them.

Partial methods provide controlled extension hooks under language-version-specific rules. Use partial for code generation or genuinely large cohesive types; splitting a class into many files is not a substitute for separating unrelated responsibilities.

variants.wording: 103. What is an Extension Method? Explain with an example.

sections.content: An extension method adds call-site syntax to an existing type without modifying it or deriving from it. Traditional syntax uses a static method in a static class with this on its first parameter. The compiler resolves it statically; it is not virtual dispatch and cannot access private internals.

For example, public static bool IsBlank(this string? value) => string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value); can be called as text.IsBlank(). It is useful for cohesive utility behavior and LINQ-style APIs. An applicable instance member normally takes precedence.

Keep extensions discoverable and narrowly scoped. They should not hide costly network or database activity behind innocent-looking property-like names. A null receiver can be passed to the method, so define and test null behavior explicitly.

variants.wording: 16. Difference between class vs record vs struct

sections.content: A class is a reference type; its default equality is reference identity unless overridden. A struct is a value type, copied by value by default. Its storage depends on context: a struct can be inside a heap object, in an array, in a register, or boxed. It is inaccurate to say every struct lives on the stack.

record class adds compiler-generated value-oriented equality, deconstruction and with-expression support. record struct supplies similar record features as a value type. Records are not automatically deeply immutable: a mutable List property remains mutable, and a with copy is shallow.

Use records for messages and DTOs where value semantics are useful. Use entity classes when identity and lifecycle dominate. Prefer small, preferably immutable structs for small values; large structs create copying costs. Equality over collection properties needs special attention because generated equality follows each property's equality implementation.

C# is a statically typed language used to build applications on .NET. The compiler normally produces intermediate language and metadata; the runtime provides execution, garbage collection and a common type system. C# is the language, while .NET includes the runtime and libraries.

For an enterprise API, C# expresses domain rules and application services, ASP.NET Core handles HTTP, and libraries provide persistence and integrations. Strong typing catches many mistakes before deployment, but it does not replace validation or tests.

Object-oriented programming models behavior and state together. Encapsulation protects invariants, abstraction exposes useful contracts, inheritance specializes an existing type, and polymorphism lets callers use different implementations through a common contract.

For example, an IPaymentGateway contract can have bank and card implementations, while an Order controls its own state transitions. Prefer composition when behavior varies independently; building a deep inheritance tree often couples unrelated concerns. OOP is useful when it clarifies business rules, not simply because every table can become a class.

Encapsulation keeps state changes behind operations that enforce rules. An Order should expose AddItem and Cancel rather than a public writable Status and unrestricted Items collection. The methods reject invalid transitions and keep the object valid after every operation.

Private fields alone are insufficient if a method returns the mutable internal list. Return a read-only view or immutable snapshot and validate all changes. This reduces the number of places developers must inspect to understand whether business invariants hold.

Inheritance creates an is-a relationship: a derived class inherits accessible members and can override virtual or abstract behavior. C# classes have one direct base class but can implement multiple interfaces. Constructors are not inherited; derived constructors can call base constructors.

Use it when the derived type can honor the base contract. A specialized pricing policy may be appropriate; inheriting a database repository just to reuse logging is usually better replaced with composition. Excessive inheritance makes changes in the base class affect many consumers unexpectedly.

Runtime polymorphism lets a call through an interface or base reference dispatch to the actual object's implementation. For example, Checkout can call gateway.PayAsync without knowing whether the gateway is a bank adapter or a test double.

Overloading is compile-time selection based on a method's signature. Overriding changes virtual dispatch; hiding with new does not. Explain this difference with a base-typed variable: an override is selected by runtime type, whereas a hidden member is selected using the reference's compile-time type.

Abstraction presents the capability callers need while concealing implementation details. IEmailSender.SendAsync expresses sending a message without exposing SMTP connections, token acquisition or provider payloads.

A good abstraction follows a real boundary that may change independently. Do not add an interface to every class by habit: a stable internal calculation may be clearer as a concrete service. Keep contracts small and explicit about failures, cancellation and side effects so implementations remain substitutable.

String is an immutable reference type: operations that appear to modify it create another string. This supports safe sharing and predictable equality by content. Repeated concatenation in a large loop can create substantial allocation pressure.

StringBuilder maintains a mutable buffer and is useful when assembling many fragments, particularly when the final length is unknown. For a few values, interpolation is clearer and often efficient. Neither choice secures SQL: always use parameters rather than building executable queries from user input.

An exception reports a failure through the call stack until a matching catch block handles it. Use try/finally or using for cleanup and catch only when you can recover, add useful context or translate at a boundary. Use throw; to preserve the current exception's stack trace.

Do not use exceptions for ordinary expected branching or swallow them with an empty catch. For an API, log unexpected failures once with a trace ID and return a safe error contract. Await asynchronous tasks so their exceptions are observed; fire-and-forget work can lose both failures and request context.

A delegate is a type-safe reference to a compatible method. Func returns a value, Action returns void, and a multicast delegate can reference multiple handlers. Delegates support callbacks and strategies without requiring a new interface for every small operation.

An event uses delegate-based notification but restricts invocation to the declaring type. Subscribers can attach and detach handlers. Unsubscribed long-lived publishers can keep subscribers alive and cause memory retention. Avoid async void handlers except where an event signature requires them, and handle their errors deliberately.

LINQ provides composable operations such as Where, Select, GroupBy and OrderBy. LINQ to Objects executes .NET delegates over objects, while a provider such as EF Core translates supported expression trees into database queries.

Many operators use deferred execution: enumeration triggers the work, potentially again on each enumeration. ToList materializes a snapshot and consumes memory. Inspect SQL for database queries and apply filtering and projection before materialization; familiar C# syntax does not guarantee an inexpensive query.

Nullable value types such as int? represent either a value or no value and expose HasValue and Value. Use pattern matching, ?? or GetValueOrDefault when absence has a defined meaning; accessing Value when empty throws.

Nullable reference annotations such as string? guide compiler flow analysis. They do not change the runtime representation or prevent null from arriving through deserialization or external libraries. Validate inputs at boundaries rather than suppressing warnings with !, and distinguish a missing value from a legitimate zero or empty string.

Generics define reusable types and methods with type parameters, such as List<T> or Result<T>. They preserve compile-time type checking and avoid the casts and many boxing costs associated with object-based collections.

Constraints express required capabilities, for example where T : class or where T : IComparable<T>. Use a generic algorithm when its logic truly applies across types. Do not force domain operations into a generic repository if the result hides important business behavior or makes queries harder to optimize.

.NET Core was the cross-platform successor to the Windows-focused .NET Framework. From .NET 5 onward, the main product uses the name .NET; ASP.NET Core and EF Core retain Core in their names. Distinguish the application's target runtime from the C# language version when discussing compatibility.

The Common Language Runtime executes managed .NET code and supplies garbage collection, exception handling, type safety and execution services. The common type system describes how types behave across .NET languages; the common language specification is a subset of conventions for interoperable public APIs.

Typically a compiler emits IL, and the JIT compiles methods to native instructions at runtime. Ahead-of-time deployment options also exist, with different compatibility and startup tradeoffs. Managed execution does not eliminate native resource leaks, data races or application-level memory retention.

variants.wording: 𝟰/ 𝗮𝘀𝘆𝗻𝗰 / 𝗮𝘄𝗮𝗶𝘁: Used to write asynchronous, non-blocking code.
2️⃣ Explain async/await and how it impacts scalability.

sections.content: An async method represents an operation whose completion may occur later. Calling it starts ordinary synchronous execution until it reaches an await whose awaiter is incomplete. The compiler rewrites the method into a state machine that records locals and the current position, arranges a continuation, and returns control to the caller. When the operation completes, the continuation resumes execution; it need not run on the original thread.

For true asynchronous network or database I/O, no application worker thread must remain blocked during the wait. That is why async APIs can serve more simultaneous requests with a bounded worker pool. Awaiting an already-completed operation may continue synchronously. async does not inherently create a thread, run in parallel, or make a CPU calculation faster.

Use Task or Task<T> for normal APIs, propagate CancellationToken, and await all owned work. Use Task.WhenAll for independent operations only when concurrency is bounded by downstream capacity. Avoid async void except event-handler contracts: its failures and completion cannot be observed like a Task.
Example

variants.wording: Task vs Thread — when would you use each?

sections.content: A Thread is an execution resource with a stack and operating-system scheduling. A Task is an abstraction for eventual completion, result, cancellation, or failure. An I/O Task can spend most of its lifetime without occupying any thread. Task.Run normally queues CPU work to the ThreadPool; it does not provide a dedicated thread.

Prefer asynchronous Task-returning APIs for database and HTTP calls. For CPU-heavy computation, consider bounded parallel processing or an external worker. Wrapping synchronous I/O in Task.Run inside ASP.NET Core merely moves blocking to another worker and rarely improves server scalability.

A dedicated Thread is an exceptional choice for a required apartment model, thread affinity, or a carefully designed long-lived blocking loop. It costs memory and scheduling overhead and needs explicit shutdown management. Tasks provide easier composition through await, WhenAll, and cancellation tokens, but cancellation remains cooperative.

variants.wording: 𝟭𝟬/ 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸: Provides exclusive access to a critical section in multithreaded code.

sections.content: lock provides exclusive entry to a critical section for threads sharing the same lock object. The compiler arranges exception-safe exit. Locking an object uses monitor synchronization; modern C# also supports specialized Lock instances with their own semantics.

Lock a private dedicated object, keep the protected region short, and maintain consistent lock ordering. Do not lock this, a public object, or an interned string because unrelated code may acquire the same lock. A process-local lock does not coordinate multiple API replicas.

You cannot await inside a lock body. Use an async-compatible primitive such as SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync and release it in finally for asynchronous mutual exclusion. For cross-instance correctness, use database constraints and transactions rather than assuming an in-memory lock protects the business operation.

variants.wording: 10. What is the difference between Task, ValueTask, and async/await?

sections.content: Task<T> is a reference representing one completion and can normally be awaited by multiple consumers. ValueTask<T> is a value type that can hold a result directly or refer to a Task or reusable completion source. It can save an allocation on a hot path that frequently completes synchronously, such as a cache lookup.

The benefit is conditional: cached Tasks already avoid some allocations, ValueTask is larger to copy, and an async state machine carrying it can grow. A ValueTask backed by IValueTaskSource generally must be consumed only once. Do not await the same instance concurrently or repeatedly; convert once with AsTask when a reusable Task is needed.

async and await are language constructs, not competing completion types. Choose Task by default, measure allocation pressure, and introduce ValueTask only when its consumer contract and performance benefit are clear.

variants.wording: 11. Why can .Result / .Wait() cause problems in ASP.NET Core applications?

sections.content: Result and Wait synchronously block a thread until a Task finishes. In a host with a single-threaded synchronization context, the blocked thread may be needed by the awaited continuation, creating a deadlock.

ASP.NET Core usually lacks that context, but blocking is still harmful: enough blocked workers cause ThreadPool starvation, queued requests and latency despite low CPU. Result and Wait can also wrap exceptions differently from await.

Await the operation, propagate cancellation and avoid Task.Run as a wrapper around every request. If a legacy dependency is unavoidably blocking, isolate it behind a bounded worker queue and capacity budget. Increasing minimum worker threads can be a measured mitigation, not a replacement for fixing blocking.

SynchronizationContext abstracts where continuations or callbacks should execute. A UI context can marshal continuation work back to the UI thread; custom test hosts can impose their own scheduling rules. Await normally considers the current context and a non-default TaskScheduler.

ASP.NET Core generally does not install the request SynchronizationContext used by classic ASP.NET. Its continuations commonly run on ThreadPool threads, so code must not assume thread affinity across await.

SynchronizationContext differs from ExecutionContext, which carries ambient data such as AsyncLocal values. Removing context capture does not automatically remove ambient state. Understand the host before diagnosing deadlocks or deciding where context preservation is necessary.

await operation.ConfigureAwait(false) tells that await not to require resumption on a captured synchronization context or non-default scheduler. It is valuable in reusable library code that has no UI or host-context dependency.

It does not start a new thread, guarantee a thread switch, suppress ExecutionContext, or fix all blocking problems. If the operation is already complete, execution can continue synchronously. In ordinary ASP.NET Core requests there is usually no special synchronization context to capture, so the impact is often small.

Application UI code should preserve context when accessing UI controls. A library can use ConfigureAwait(false) consistently on its internal awaits while exposing normal Task-returning methods. The preferred remedy for sync-over-async remains making the call chain asynchronous.

variants.wording: Thread starvation and how to identify it
How would you troubleshoot thread starvation?

sections.content: The .NET ThreadPool reuses worker threads to execute queued work and many task continuations. It adjusts worker supply according to runtime heuristics. ThreadPool starvation means runnable work waits too long for available workers, often because workers are blocked; it can occur with low CPU usage.

The ThreadPool reuses worker threads for callbacks and scheduled work. Starvation occurs when available workers cannot make progress on queued work, commonly because many are blocked on synchronous I/O, locks or Task.Wait.

Look at rising queue length, thread count, poor completion rate and latency together; low CPU does not rule it out. Use dotnet-counters to establish trends, then dotnet-stack, traces or a dump to find stacks blocked in waits or synchronous calls. Compare before and after the regression and distinguish starvation from CPU saturation.

Replace sync-over-async with await, shorten locks, bound concurrent dependencies and remove unnecessary blocking. Measure p95/p99 and throughput after the fix. Tune ThreadPool settings only with load-test evidence and rollback criteria because more threads can worsen memory use and contention.

variants.wording: 6️⃣ How does Garbage Collection work in .NET?

sections.content: The GC finds managed objects reachable from roots such as stacks, statics and handles. Unreachable objects can be reclaimed; it does not simply delete everything whose method has returned. Generations 0, 1 and 2 favor collecting short-lived objects cheaply, while long-lived survivors cost more to scan.

Large objects and pinned objects have additional heap behavior. Collections can include stop-the-world phases even with background GC. Managed memory leaks occur when unwanted objects remain reachable through static caches, event subscriptions or collections.

IDisposable handles deterministic cleanup of resources such as streams and native handles; GC is not timely resource cleanup. Diagnose allocation rate, live heap size, generation collections and pause time before tuning GC. Avoid routinely calling GC.Collect in request handling because it usually disrupts the runtime's adaptive behavior.

Span<T> is a ref struct describing a contiguous region of memory without copying it. It can view an array, stack-allocated storage or certain unmanaged memory. ReadOnlySpan<T> offers a read-only view and is useful for parsing slices without allocating substrings.

Its lifetime restrictions prevent references from escaping valid storage. In supported newer language versions it can be used in some async-method regions, but cannot live across an await or yield suspension. Use Memory<T> when the buffer must be retained across asynchronous work.

A span does not own or extend the lifetime of its storage. Use it on measured parsing or binary-processing hot paths, validate bounds, and prefer ordinary collections elsewhere. Stackalloc should be small and bounded to avoid stack overflow.

ArrayPool<T> rents reusable buffers, reducing repeated allocation and GC pressure for high-volume serialization or I/O. Rent may return an array larger than requested and containing old data, so process only the valid length.

Return the buffer in finally after all consumers finish, and never retain or access it afterward. Clear sensitive contents or use Return(clearArray: true) as appropriate. Do not return the same buffer twice or let an asynchronous operation outlive the rental.

Pooling trades allocation cost for ownership complexity and retained memory. It helps large frequent buffers, but is unnecessary for many tiny or infrequent allocations. Test error and cancellation paths as carefully as the successful path.

FrozenDictionary<TKey,TValue> builds an immutable dictionary optimized for a read-heavy workload after construction. Construction can be more expensive than Dictionary, making it suitable for long-lived routing metadata, reference data or lookup tables loaded once.

Dictionary is mutable and cheap to update. Concurrent readers are safe only if no one mutates it and publication is safe; concurrent writes require synchronization or ConcurrentDictionary. A frozen dictionary can be shared for reads, but mutable objects stored as values are not themselves frozen.

Use ToFrozenDictionary after loading and validating the final data. Benchmark actual key types, sizes and comparers; frozen is not universally faster for every case. It is available in modern .NET, so check the project's target framework.

Concurrency means several operations are in progress over overlapping time. Parallelism means work executes simultaneously on multiple processing resources. An asynchronous API can be highly concurrent while mostly waiting on I/O and using few threads.

For independent network calls, start a bounded number and await them. For CPU-heavy work, use parallel processing with a degree of parallelism aligned to available cores and workload. More Tasks do not automatically mean more useful parallelism.

Unbounded fan-out exhausts sockets, memory, database connections and downstream quotas. Define cancellation, error aggregation and ordering needs. In a web server, avoid multiplying per-request parallelism across thousands of requests without an overall admission-control budget.

variants.wording: Explain the ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline.
1. Explain the complete ASP.NET Core request pipeline. How does Middleware execute?

sections.content: Kestrel accepts the HTTP request and the application processes it through ordered middleware. Each middleware can act before next, call the next delegate, act after next, or short-circuit. Response processing therefore unwinds in reverse order. Endpoint routing selects endpoint metadata; the endpoint ultimately runs MVC, a minimal API or another handler.

Typical ordering places production exception handling early, HTTPS handling as appropriate, routing, CORS where required, authentication, authorization and endpoint execution. Static files and response caching need deliberate placement because they may short-circuit or expose content. Exact ordering depends on the features enabled.

An endpoint may bind inputs, validate them, execute business logic and serialize a result. Authentication and authorization are not controller business logic. To troubleshoot order-dependent behavior, log entry/exit with trace IDs and inspect the selected endpoint metadata.

questions.title: Dependency injection lifetimes

variants.wording: What are Transient, Scoped, and Singleton DI lifetimes?
3. Explain Dependency Injection lifetimes: Transient vs Scoped vs Singleton. What problems can occur with incorrect lifetimes?
14. Explain Transient, Scoped, and Singleton with a real production scenario.

sections.content: Transient creates a new instance for each resolution. Scoped reuses one instance within an explicit IServiceScope; HTTP requests usually have their own scope. Singleton reuses one instance per root service provider, not one instance across every server in a cluster.

A practical request may use a scoped DbContext and business service, a transient stateless formatter, and a singleton immutable metadata cache. Singletons must tolerate concurrent requests. A scoped DbContext is not thread-safe and should not be used concurrently even inside one request.

A singleton capturing a scoped object stretches its lifetime and can leak tenant or user state. Disposable transients resolved from the root may also remain retained until shutdown. Pick lifetimes based on ownership and concurrency, enable scope validation, and let the container dispose objects it creates.

references: Further reading: ASP.NET Core dependency injection

variants.wording: Why do we use DTOs instead of exposing EF Core entities directly?

sections.content: A DTO is the explicit input or output contract of an API. EF entities describe persistence and relationships; exposing them directly couples clients to schema changes and can reveal internal columns, tenant identifiers or navigation graphs.

Use separate request and response DTOs, validate input and map only permitted fields. This prevents mass assignment of server-owned properties and lets responses evolve independently. Projection with Select can build response DTOs in SQL, reducing columns transferred and avoiding unnecessary tracking.

Mapping adds code and must be maintained, but it is valuable at external boundaries. A DTO alone does not enforce security: authorization and tenant filters remain necessary. Avoid returning cyclic navigation graphs or relying on serializer settings to define the public contract accidentally.

variants.wording: How do you implement global exception handling in ASP.NET Core?
15. How would you implement Global Exception Handling in ASP.NET Core? Middleware or Exception Filter? Why?
8️⃣ How would you implement global exception handling?

sections.content: Use exception-handling middleware or IExceptionHandler to translate unhandled failures into a consistent ProblemDetails response. Map expected domain outcomes deliberately: validation to 400 or 422 according to the API contract, missing resources to 404 and a state conflict to 409. Unexpected failures return 500 with a trace identifier rather than stack traces.

Place global handling early enough to cover downstream middleware and endpoints. MVC exception filters are useful for MVC-specific policies but do not cover every upstream or response-writing failure. Once response headers have started, replacing the response may no longer be possible.

Log once at the appropriate boundary with safe context, preserve the original stack, and distinguish client cancellation from server faults. Test both development and production behavior and avoid reporting every exception as a successful HTTP 200 response.

variants.wording: 97. Can you use a concrete class instead of an interface for Dependency Injection?

sections.content: Yes. services.AddScoped<ReportService>() allows ReportService to be injected directly. Dependency injection does not require an interface; it requires dependencies to be supplied externally rather than hard-coded construction inside business logic.

Use an interface when there is a meaningful contract, multiple implementations, an infrastructure boundary or useful substitution in tests. A simple concrete collaborator can be entirely appropriate and avoids empty interfaces created only for convention.

Concrete injection does not make every member mockable with every mocking library. Design tests around behavior and consider extracting external effects behind interfaces. Whichever form is chosen, the lifetime, thread safety and ownership rules remain the same.

variants.wording: 2. Middleware vs Filters — what is the difference and when would you use each?

sections.content: Middleware operates at the HTTP pipeline level and can cover MVC, minimal APIs and static resources. MVC filters operate within the MVC action pipeline: authorization, resource, action, exception and result filters have different scopes. Minimal API endpoint filters are another mechanism; they are not identical to MVC filters.

Use middleware for broad correlation, global exception translation, request timing or security infrastructure. Use an action filter for MVC-specific argument handling or action/result behavior. An exception filter does not catch every failure elsewhere in the middleware pipeline and is therefore insufficient as the sole global error handler.

Avoid duplicating authorization logic in custom filters when policy-based authorization fits. Keep cross-cutting behavior testable and document order, especially where a component can short-circuit execution.

variants.wording: 4. What happens internally when you register a service using AddScoped()?

sections.content: AddScoped registers a ServiceDescriptor describing service type, implementation type or factory, and scoped lifetime. It does not normally instantiate the service when registration executes. Building the provider prepares resolution machinery; the first resolution within a scope creates the instance and subsequent resolutions reuse that scope's instance.

Constructor dependencies are resolved recursively. An implementation factory is invoked for the scope's first creation. A new scope has a separate instance; scopes are not magically nested ownership hierarchies. Disposal of the scope disposes tracked disposable services.

Use scoped services for a unit of work or request-specific state. Resolving one from the root can cause a captive lifetime or a validation exception. Registering a service and manually constructing it elsewhere bypasses these ownership guarantees.

variants.wording: 5. Why should you NOT inject a Scoped service directly into a Singleton?

sections.content: A singleton lives as long as the root provider while a scoped dependency belongs to a shorter scope. Direct capture breaks that ownership model: a DbContext may retain stale tracked entities, be accessed concurrently or carry state between tenants.

With scope validation enabled, resolving this invalid graph typically throws. Without it, a scoped object resolved from the root can effectively live until application shutdown. The problem is not solved by changing only the interface or adding a lock.

For background work, inject IServiceScopeFactory, create a scope per work item, resolve the scoped service inside it and await completion before disposal. Do not capture HttpContext. Pass explicit immutable job data, tenant identity and cancellation into the operation.

variants.wording: 8. What is the difference between IServiceCollection and IServiceProvider?

sections.content: Dependency injection supplies collaborators from outside a class, typically through constructors. IServiceCollection is the registration list configured at startup. IServiceProvider is the built resolver that creates and supplies those services according to their lifetimes.

The provider can call constructors and factories and track disposal, but cannot decide correct business boundaries. Keep constructors explicit so dependencies are visible. Avoid calling BuildServiceProvider during registration because it can create duplicate singleton graphs and confusing disposal.

Prefer constructor injection over passing IServiceProvider everywhere, which hides dependencies as a service locator. Use scopes or explicit factories at composition boundaries when runtime selection is genuinely needed. Registration order also matters when resolving multiple implementations.

variants.wording: 9. IEnumerable<T> vs IAsyncEnumerable<T> — when would you use each in an API?

sections.content: IEnumerable<T> retrieves each next item synchronously. IAsyncEnumerable<T> allows MoveNextAsync to await I/O and supports await foreach, useful for database or network streams that arrive over time. It is different from Task<List<T>>, which completes after the whole list has been materialized.

Streaming can reduce peak memory and time to first item, but the database connection and scope may remain open while the client consumes the response. Proxies, serializers and clients can also buffer, so verify end-to-end behavior. Pagination is often simpler for interactive clients.

Pass cancellation to the enumeration, avoid sharing one DbContext across concurrent enumerators and plan failures after headers have been sent. You cannot always replace a partially streamed success response with a clean error document.

variants.wording: 12. How does ASP.NET Core handle configuration? Explain IConfiguration, Options Pattern, and IOptions<T>.
13. What is the difference between IOptions<T>, IOptionsSnapshot<T>, and IOptionsMonitor<T>?

sections.content: IConfiguration merges configured providers such as JSON, environment variables and command-line arguments; later providers commonly override earlier keys. Bind related settings into a typed options class and validate required values and ranges, ideally at startup.

IOptions<T> exposes a stable options value and is suitable for ordinary fixed configuration. IOptionsSnapshot<T> is scoped and recomputes per scope when supported providers have changed. IOptionsMonitor<T> is singleton-compatible and supports current values and change notifications. Reload works only when the underlying provider supplies change information.

Do not treat options as a secret store or assume every setting updates live. Some resources must be rebuilt safely when settings change. Avoid logging secrets, validate replacement values, and use Key Vault or managed identity for sensitive configuration.

variants.wording: 16. What is Endpoint Routing, and how is it different from traditional MVC routing?

sections.content: Endpoint routing separates matching from execution. Matching selects an endpoint and its metadata so intervening middleware can apply authorization, CORS and other policies before execution. This unifies routing across controllers, minimal APIs and other endpoint types.

Traditional MVC routing focused on selecting controller actions within MVC. Modern controller routing still supports conventional routes and attribute routes, but they participate in the endpoint system. Attribute routing places templates such as [HttpGet("orders/{id:int}")] close to the action.

Route constraints help match shape; they are not a complete validation or security mechanism. Use stable resource-oriented routes, avoid ambiguous templates, and distinguish 404 from unsupported-method behavior when debugging.

variants.wording: 17. Explain Model Binding vs Model Validation. Where does each happen in the request pipeline?

sections.content: Model binding maps HTTP input into parameters and models. [FromRoute], [FromQuery], [FromBody] and [FromForm] explicitly select sources; body formatters deserialize formats such as JSON. Binding errors include malformed numbers or invalid JSON.

Validation checks the resulting model against declared rules and application constraints. With [ApiController], invalid ModelState normally produces an automatic 400 response. Business invariants such as a payment exceeding the available balance still belong in application/domain logic and may require database checks.

Binding and validation occur after routing in endpoint processing, before the action's main work. Do not bind persistence entities directly because clients may overpost protected fields. Validate size, ranges and allowed values, and return consistent field-level error information.

HttpClient should reuse connections rather than create a fresh handler per request. Use IHttpClientFactory with named/typed clients, or a carefully configured long-lived client with SocketsHttpHandler.PooledConnectionLifetime to allow DNS changes to take effect.

Configure per-dependency time budgets, cancellation, response disposal and bounded concurrency. Factory-created clients can be short-lived because the factory pools handlers. Do not capture a typed client indefinitely without considering handler lifetime and DNS behavior.

Retry only appropriate failures and replayable requests, honor server throttling and protect non-idempotent operations. Avoid storing request-specific headers on a shared client in ways that race across users. Record dependency duration and result without logging authorization tokens.

variants.wording: 1️⃣1️⃣ How would you design an idempotent API?
Q3. Users occasionally submit the same payment request multiple times. How would you prevent duplicate processing?

sections.content: An idempotent operation has the same intended effect when repeated. For payment POST requests, accept an idempotency key scoped to the authenticated customer and operation. Persist the key, a request fingerprint and processing/result state under a unique database constraint.

The first request reserves the key and performs the operation; retries with the same payload receive the stored result or an explicit in-progress response. Reusing a key with a different payload must be rejected. Concurrent requests must race against the database constraint, not a memory-only check.

Forward a stable key to the payment provider and reconcile uncertain outcomes when a network timeout occurs after a possible charge. Define retention and retry semantics. HTTP method conventions alone do not prevent duplicate charges, and blindly retrying a payment can make the problem worse.

variants.wording: 1️⃣2️⃣ How would you handle API versioning?

sections.content: Version when a change breaks a published contract, such as removing a field, changing meaning or requiring new input. Additive compatible changes often do not require a new version. Choose an explicit route, header or media-type policy and document it consistently.

Keep supported versions testable with contract tests and separate OpenAPI descriptions. Reuse domain logic while adapting old and new contracts at the boundary; duplicating entire implementations increases divergence. Publish deprecation dates and observe real client use before retiring a version.
A version number alone does not guarantee compatibility. Authentication rules, error shapes, paging and defaults are also part of the contract. Avoid silently switching old clients to new semantics.

variants.wording: Q4. A background task takes several minutes to complete and should not block the API response. How would you design it in .NET?

sections.content: Accept and validate the request, persist a durable job record and publish work reliably, typically using an outbox. Return 202 Accepted with a job identifier and a status URL. The API request ends while a worker processes the job.

A worker or Function claims work, updates progress, honors cancellation where meaningful and retries transient failures. Completion records must be idempotent because a worker can crash after committing work but before acknowledging its message. Store input references rather than huge message payloads.

Use authentication on status and result endpoints and include tenant ownership. Define expiration, poison-job handling and restart behavior. An in-memory channel is fine only when loss on process restart is acceptable; it is not equivalent to durable processing.

variants.wording: Q6. You need different implementations of the same service for different customers or business conditions. How would you design this using dependency injection?

sections.content: Model the varying behavior as a strategy, such as IPriceCalculator with customer-specific implementations. Resolve a strategy through an explicit selector/factory keyed by an authorized business condition; modern .NET also supports keyed registrations and keyed injection.

Keep common workflow in the application service and varying rules inside the strategies. Do not let an untrusted request pick an arbitrary tenant implementation without validating the tenant and entitlement. Avoid injecting IServiceProvider into every domain class just to switch services.

Prefer a scoped selector when its strategies use scoped dependencies. Test each implementation against the same behavioral contract and test the selection logic separately. For a small stable choice, a simple explicit dictionary or switch at the composition boundary is clearer than reflection-based plugins.

IHostedService defines StartAsync and StopAsync for work managed by the application host. BackgroundService implements that contract and provides ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken) for a long-running loop, making it convenient for queue consumers and periodic processing.

Both normally live for the host lifetime and must manage scoped dependencies explicitly through per-operation scopes. Observe cancellation, handle exceptions deliberately and stop within the configured shutdown budget. Runtime details of startup and ExecuteAsync scheduling vary by .NET version; do not rely on blocking startup behavior.

A hosted service inside an API is not automatically durable and runs on each replica. For critical jobs, use a durable queue, idempotent processing and a separately scalable worker if needed. A fire-and-forget Task tied to a request is not a reliable replacement.

variants.wording: 51. What is Rate Limiting and its types?

sections.content: Rate limits constrain how much work a caller can submit; concurrency limits constrain work in flight. Fixed-window algorithms count within time buckets, sliding windows reduce boundary bursts, token buckets permit bounded bursts, and concurrency limiters cap simultaneous operations.

Partition limits by authenticated identity, tenant, subscription or another trustworthy key. Return 429 for rate exhaustion with retry guidance when possible. Bound queues so overload does not just accumulate latency and memory. Distinguish per-user quotas from global protection of a database or model endpoint.

The built-in in-process limiter does not automatically enforce one shared quota across multiple replicas. A gateway or distributed coordinator may be needed. Test burst and abuse scenarios and avoid trusting a spoofable header as the sole client identity.

Use structured logs with named fields such as order ID, event ID and trace ID rather than concatenated text. Log meaningful state transitions and failures at appropriate levels, and correlate logs with distributed traces and metrics.

Do not log access tokens, passwords or unrestricted request bodies. Define retention, access controls and sampling appropriate to the data. Avoid logging the same exception at every layer; a boundary with useful context is usually the best place.

A log stream that looks normal does not prove the application is healthy. Missing instrumentation, excessive sampling or waits without exceptions can hide latency problems, so combine logs with request and dependency measurements.

Kestrel is ASP.NET Core's cross-platform web server. It can serve requests directly or operate behind a reverse proxy that handles edge concerns such as TLS termination, routing or process integration.

Hosting choices include managed application platforms, containers and IIS integration on Windows. In-process IIS hosting and out-of-process forwarding differ, so describe the actual deployment rather than assuming every IIS request uses the same path.

Configure trusted forwarded headers, graceful shutdown, health checks and request limits. The reverse proxy and application must agree on scheme and client addressing; trusting arbitrary forwarded headers can create security problems.
ASP.NET Core uses an environment name such as Development, Staging or Production to select environment-specific behavior and configuration. The name is configuration, not a security boundary.

Keep developer exception details and development-only endpoints out of production. Load secrets through suitable providers and validate required options at startup. Prefer the same application artifact across environments with controlled external configuration.

When diagnosing a production-only problem, compare effective settings, identity, networking and feature flags rather than only source code. Do not assume an environment-specific JSON file is the only configuration source; later providers can override it.
Three concrete approaches are inline app.Use delegates, a conventional class with Invoke or InvokeAsync registered through UseMiddleware<T>, and factory-activated middleware implementing IMiddleware.

Inline middleware is convenient for a small local concern. Conventional class middleware supports reusable components, while IMiddleware enables container-controlled per-request activation and scoped constructor dependencies. An extension method such as UseMyFeature is a packaging convenience, not by itself a separate execution mechanism.

Call and await next when the request should continue, and understand what short-circuiting excludes. Conventional middleware constructors should not capture scoped services; inject them into InvokeAsync or use IMiddleware when appropriate.

A web API exposes capabilities over HTTP to clients. It may use REST conventions but not every HTTP JSON endpoint is fully RESTful. REST emphasizes resources, a uniform interface, stateless requests, cacheability and layered systems.

Use methods consistently: GET reads without intended state changes, POST submits work or creates subordinate resources, PUT replaces the addressed resource and DELETE removes it. Choose status codes, representations and links that communicate the outcome.

Statelessness means each request contains the necessary context; it does not forbid durable server-side application data. Design resource authorization, pagination, error contracts and idempotency alongside routes. Avoid claiming that using JSON and GET/POST alone guarantees REST compliance.

IActionResult describes an MVC result that executes into an HTTP response. ActionResult<T> combines a documented successful payload type with other results such as NotFound. Minimal APIs also offer IResult and typed result types.

Use 200 for a successful representation, 201 with a resource location after creation, 202 for accepted asynchronous work, and 204 when no body is returned. Use 400 for malformed/invalid requests, 401 when authentication is needed or invalid, 403 for insufficient permission, 404 for missing resources, 409 for conflicts, and 429 for throttling.
Status codes must match behavior and should not encode every failure as 200. Keep error payloads consistent with ProblemDetails and avoid returning a stack trace or sensitive existence information.

OpenAPI is a machine-readable description of API paths, parameters, schemas, responses and security requirements. Swagger commonly refers to tools such as Swagger UI that visualize and let developers exercise that description.

Generate the specification from endpoints and enrich it with useful response models and examples. Validate it in CI or use contract tests to detect incompatible changes. Authentication shown in Swagger UI does not itself protect the backend; the API still enforces policies.

Restrict interactive documentation where required by the environment and never embed production credentials in examples. Treat generated docs as part of the API contract, not proof that every behavior has been tested.

Serialization converts an object representation to a wire format such as JSON; deserialization builds a model from that format. ASP.NET Core commonly uses System.Text.Json, with configurable naming, enum and date behavior.

Public contracts should explicitly define null handling, numeric precision, property names and backward compatibility. Use DTOs to avoid accidental navigation cycles or exposure of internal entity state. Do not enable unsafe polymorphic deserialization from untrusted type names.

Large payloads affect CPU, allocations and latency. Project only needed fields, paginate or stream when appropriate, and consider source-generated serializers for measured startup or throughput needs. Validate payload sizes and malformed input.

variants.wording: 53. What is Method Injection in Controller?

sections.content: Controller action method injection supplies a dependency only to the action that needs it, commonly using [FromServices]. This differs from [FromBody] or [FromQuery], which bind caller input rather than resolve services.

Constructor injection is clearer when most actions share the dependency and makes the controller's full dependency set visible. Method injection can keep a rarely used expensive or specialized dependency local to one action.

The dependency retains its registered lifetime and is resolved within the request's provider. Avoid accepting untrusted input that chooses arbitrary registered types. Test action behavior with explicit collaborators rather than using a service locator throughout the method.

Compression reduces transferred bytes for suitable text responses such as JSON, HTML and CSS. It trades CPU for bandwidth and can improve latency on slower networks. Already-compressed images and archives usually gain little.

Configure supported encodings and MIME types and avoid double compression between a proxy and application. Measure response size and CPU at load. Streaming and very small responses may have different tradeoffs.

Consider information-leak risks when compressing secret-bearing responses mixed with attacker-controlled content over HTTPS. Compression is a targeted optimization, not a replacement for projecting smaller DTOs and limiting result size.

variants.wording: What is the N+1 query problem, and how do you solve it?

sections.content: The N+1 problem occurs when one query loads N parents and another query runs for each parent's related data. With 100 orders, reading each customer's details can produce 101 database round trips even when every individual query is fast.

Detect it through query counts and distributed traces. Fix it with a projection that retrieves exactly the response shape, suitable eager loading, or a deliberate batch query. Do not blindly Include every relationship: excessive joins can multiply data. Validate both database execution time and transferred rows under realistic cardinality.

variants.wording: A SQL query is taking 10 seconds. How would you troubleshoot and optimize it?
How to investigate a slow query
17️⃣ A query is taking 10 seconds in production. How do you troubleshoot it?

sections.content: First capture the exact SQL, parameters, duration, execution count and context from a slow trace. Separate connection-pool waiting, blocking, execution, network transfer and application materialization. A ten-second API request does not prove the SQL statement itself took ten seconds.

Inspect the actual execution plan and Query Store history, comparing estimated and actual row counts. Look for scans, expensive sorts, spills, stale statistics, parameter-sensitive behavior and predicates that prevent useful index seeks. Check locks, wait types, logical reads and the volume of returned data.

Apply the smallest evidence-backed change: a suitable index, a selective projection, pagination, a rewritten predicate or fewer round trips. Test representative parameters and concurrency, measure reads and latency, and verify write overhead. Do not add indexes or query hints without understanding their system-wide cost.

variants.wording: Write SQL to find the second-highest salary.

sections.content: Clarify that the requirement is the second-highest distinct non-null salary. DENSE_RANK can return all employees tied at that salary. If fewer than two distinct values exist, the query below returns no rows.

A scalar alternative is MAX(Salary) where Salary is less than the overall maximum; that returns NULL if no second value exists. Using OFFSET 1 without deduplicating first may simply select another employee with the highest salary.

variants.wording: 105. What is the difference between a Temporary Table and CTE?

sections.content: A common table expression is a named query expression scoped to the immediately following statement. It improves readability and supports recursion, but is not a guarantee of materialization or a cached result.

A temporary table stores rows in tempdb, can be indexed and can be reused across statements within its lifetime. It can help when an intermediate dataset benefits from statistics or repeated access, at the cost of writes and management overhead. Choose based on execution plans and data size, not a rule that one is always faster.

variants.wording: 106. What is ROW_NUMBER() in SQL? Explain with a real-time example.

sections.content: ROW_NUMBER assigns a unique sequential number within each partition using the specified ordering. It is useful for choosing the latest row per customer or numbering a result set. If the ORDER BY values tie, add a stable unique tiebreaker for deterministic results.

Window functions do not themselves filter rows, so put the numbered result in a CTE or subquery and then filter. For large paginated APIs, keyset pagination may scale better than calculating or skipping increasingly large row counts.
Example

WITH Latest AS (
    SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, CreatedAt,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
             PARTITION BY CustomerId
             ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC, OrderId DESC) AS rn
    FROM dbo.Orders
)
SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, CreatedAt
FROM Latest WHERE rn = 1;

variants.wording: 107. What is the difference between RANK() and DENSE_RANK()?

sections.content: Both functions give equal ordering values the same rank. RANK leaves gaps after ties: salaries 100, 100 and 90 produce ranks 1, 1 and 3. DENSE_RANK produces 1, 1 and 2, which is useful when asking for the second distinct salary.

ROW_NUMBER instead gives each row a different number and requires a deterministic tiebreaker when selecting one record. Clarify whether an interview question means the second employee, the second distinct value or every employee tied at that value.

variants.wording: 108. What are Magic Tables in SQL Server?

sections.content: SQL Server DML triggers can use the logical inserted and deleted tables. INSERT supplies new rows in inserted, DELETE supplies old rows in deleted, and UPDATE supplies both before and after values.

A trigger fires for a statement and may receive many rows. Write set-based logic that joins these tables by key; assigning one row to a scalar variable silently mishandles multi-row operations. Keep triggers short and avoid remote side effects because they run within the triggering transaction and can extend locks or cause failures.

variants.wording: 109. What is a Deadlock? How do you identify and resolve it?

sections.content: A deadlock is a cycle of transactions waiting for resources held by each other. SQL Server chooses a victim and rolls back that transaction. It differs from ordinary blocking, where progress can resume when one holder finishes.

Capture the deadlock graph using Extended Events and identify statements, locks, access order and transaction scope. Standardize resource acquisition order, shorten transactions and add useful indexes to reduce the locked footprint. Retry a deadlock victim's whole transaction with bounded backoff only when replay is safe. Increasing timeouts does not remove a lock cycle.

variants.wording: 110. What is WITH (NOLOCK) in SQL Server? When should you use it, and what are its risks?

sections.content: WITH (NOLOCK) requests Read Uncommitted semantics for data reads. It can return dirty data, miss rows or return rows more than once under concurrent modifications. It still takes some locks, including schema-stability locks, so it is not a universal no-blocking switch.

Do not use it to make financial, inventory or authorization queries appear faster. Investigate blocking and indexing, shorten transactions, or evaluate row-versioned isolation for consistent reads. Consider NOLOCK only when explicitly accepting inconsistent results in a suitable noncritical workload and documenting that tradeoff.

questions.title: Optimistic concurrency

variants.wording: 20. What happens when multiple API requests simultaneously update the same database record? How would you handle concurrency?
Q7. Two users update the same database record at the same time. How would you handle concurrency in Entity Framework Core?

sections.content: Without a concurrency check, two updates can overwrite each other with last-writer-wins behavior. For SQL Server and EF Core, map a rowversion column as a concurrency token. EF includes the original token in the update predicate; zero affected rows cause DbUpdateConcurrencyException.

Handle the conflict deliberately: reload current values, ask the user to merge, or retry a safe operation after recomputing it against fresh state. An API can return 409 Conflict or use an ETag and If-Match with 412. Do not blindly replay a stale full entity, and use atomic database operations or constraints for inventory and uniqueness invariants.

variants.wording: 16️⃣ What happens when an index is added to a large table?

sections.content: An index maintains a searchable structure over chosen columns so SQL Server can locate relevant rows without scanning the entire table. Key order matters for filtering and ordering; included columns can cover a query without becoming search keys.

Indexes consume storage and must be maintained for inserts, updates and deletes. Too many indexes increase write latency, log volume and maintenance cost. An index on a low-selectivity predicate may not be useful, and functions or implicit conversions can prevent efficient access.

Adding an index to a large table consumes CPU, I/O, transaction log and potentially tempdb, with locking behavior depending on the operation and available features. Plan and test the build, assess online/resumable support for the environment, and monitor impact. An index being available never guarantees the optimizer will choose it.

Define the business key before identifying duplicates. Two employees sharing a name are not necessarily duplicates; a tenant identifier and external reference may be a more appropriate key. GROUP BY and HAVING locate repeated keys without deleting anything.

When cleanup is required, use ROW_NUMBER with a deterministic keeper rule, review affected records and perform the change transactionally. Add a unique constraint afterward if that key must remain unique; application-side checks alone can race under concurrent requests.
Example

SELECT TenantId, ExternalReference, COUNT(*) AS DuplicateCount
FROM dbo.Orders
GROUP BY TenantId, ExternalReference
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

INNER JOIN returns matching combinations from both inputs. LEFT JOIN also preserves rows from the left input that have no match, filling right-side columns with NULL. One-to-many matches can multiply rows, which matters for totals and pagination.

A right-side predicate in WHERE may remove the unmatched rows and effectively turn a left join into an inner join. Put a predicate in ON when it should restrict matches while retaining all left rows. Use NOT EXISTS for many anti-join requirements and be careful with NULL semantics.

Other join forms include RIGHT JOIN, which preserves the right input; FULL OUTER JOIN, which preserves unmatched rows from both; and CROSS JOIN, which returns combinations. A self-join joins a table to another reference to itself, such as employees to managers.
Example

SELECT c.CustomerId, o.OrderId
FROM dbo.Customers AS c
LEFT JOIN dbo.Orders AS o
  ON o.CustomerId = c.CustomerId AND o.Status = 'Open';

variants.wording: 18️⃣ Explain ACID properties and database normalization.

sections.content: Atomicity means a transaction commits all its changes or none. Consistency means valid constraints and invariants remain satisfied. Isolation controls how concurrent transactions observe one another. Durability means committed changes survive failures according to the database's configured guarantees.

For a transfer, debit and credit should be in one local transaction with suitable checks. Isolation is not the same as running every transaction serially; weaker levels permit more concurrency and particular anomalies. ACID in one database does not automatically cover an HTTP call or another service's database.

Normalization is a schema-design discipline that reduces duplicated facts and update anomalies, rather than a transaction guarantee. Separate customers from orders when customer details have one current authoritative value, while deliberately retaining a historical shipping address when the business requires it. The normalization section explains first, second and third normal forms in more detail.

EF Core is an object-relational mapper that maps .NET entities to database tables, translates LINQ queries and coordinates changes through DbContext. It reduces repetitive persistence code but does not remove the need to understand SQL and transaction behavior.

Project only needed columns, use asynchronous I/O and examine generated SQL for important paths. Migrations manage schema evolution; they are not a substitute for deployment planning. Use direct SQL or a specialized data-access tool where a measured requirement justifies it, while retaining parameterization and transaction discipline.

DbContext represents a unit of work with configuration, a change tracker and access to mapped entity sets. DbSet<TEntity> provides a query and change entry point for one entity type; it is not an in-memory copy of the entire table.

In an HTTP application, use a short-lived context, normally scoped to a request. DbContext is not thread-safe: do not execute parallel operations on one instance. Await each operation or create independent contexts when parallel work is justified. Dispose contexts and avoid carrying tracked entities across unrelated requests.

A migration records schema changes derived from the model, while a model snapshot supports generating subsequent differences. Review the generated migration and SQL because an apparently small property change can drop data, rebuild an index or lock a large table.

For production, deploy reviewed scripts or a controlled migration job. Use expand-and-contract changes: add a compatible column, deploy readers/writers that support both versions, backfill, and remove old structures later. Test on realistic data and define recovery. Automatically running migrations on every service instance can create contention and uncontrolled rollout risk.

Eager loading fetches related entities as part of the planned query, commonly through Include. Explicit loading requests a relationship later through the context. Lazy loading fetches it when accessed when the required configuration is enabled.

Lazy loading can hide network I/O inside property access and cause N+1 queries during serialization. Eager loading multiple collections may produce large joined result sets. Prefer DTO projections for APIs; assess split queries when joins multiply rows, while considering extra round trips and consistency across those queries.

Tracked queries register entities with the DbContext so changes can be detected and persisted through SaveChanges. Tracking also performs identity resolution, returning the same tracked instance for a given key within that context.

AsNoTracking is useful for read-only work because it avoids normal tracking overhead. It does not automatically make every query faster, especially where repeated entities benefit from identity resolution; AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution is another option. For API responses, projection can be more important than the tracking choice. Attach detached updates carefully to avoid unintended writes.
A unit of work tracks related changes and commits them together. DbContext provides this behavior, and one SaveChanges call is normally transactional for providers that support transactions.

Use an explicit transaction when multiple database operations must succeed together, while keeping its duration short. A unit of work does not automatically make a database write and a Service Bus publish atomic. For that boundary, persist an outbox record in the same database transaction and publish asynchronously.

A navigation property expresses a relationship between entities, such as Order.Customer or Customer.Orders. The foreign key stores the relationship in the database; the navigation gives code an object-oriented way to traverse it.

Relationship fix-up can populate navigations for entities already tracked, so a populated property does not necessarily mean a new query ran. Conversely, an unpopulated collection may simply not have been loaded. Avoid serializing entities directly because navigation cycles, excessive loading and accidental data exposure complicate API contracts.

A shadow property exists in EF Core's model and change tracker without a corresponding CLR property. It is useful for persistence concerns such as an audit field or a foreign key that is intentionally absent from the domain class.

Configure it in model building and access it through the context entry or EF.Property in queries. Because its value is tracker/model based rather than an ordinary object member, detached or no-tracking workflows need special care. Use it sparingly where hiding persistence detail improves the model rather than obscuring important business state.

SQL Server is a relational database platform that stores related data in tables and supports SQL queries, transactions, constraints, indexes and operational tooling. The database engine enforces consistency even when many application instances access the same data.

For a .NET service, model keys and constraints around business invariants, choose suitable data types and keep transactions short. Connection pooling belongs to the client provider, while query optimization and locking are engine concerns. A database that is fast in development can behave differently with production data distributions and concurrency.

Normalization structures relational data to reduce duplication and update anomalies. First normal form avoids repeating groups and uses values appropriate to each attribute's domain.
