Second normal form removes partial dependency on a composite candidate key; third normal form removes inappropriate transitive dependencies among non-key attributes.

For example, keep customer contact details in Customers and reference the customer from Orders, rather than rewriting the address in every order unless an immutable historical shipping address is required. Denormalize only for an explicit read or history requirement, with a clear owner and process for maintaining consistency.

Denormalization deliberately stores redundant or precomputed data, such as a reporting summary, to simplify or accelerate reads. It introduces write and reconciliation work, so identify the authoritative source and how updates reach the redundant representation.

A clustered index organizes a table's data at its leaf level, so a table has at most one. A nonclustered index is a separate structure containing its key and a row locator, plus optional included columns.

Choose a stable, reasonably narrow clustered key because its value can appear in nonclustered indexes. A primary key does not inherently have to be clustered. Design indexes for actual predicates, joins and ordering rather than assuming every column should have one. Heaps, clustered columnstore and specialized indexes are separate design choices with different workloads.

A primary key uniquely identifies a row and does not permit null values. A foreign key enforces that a referenced key exists, subject to its nullable and constraint configuration. Together they protect relationships even when writes bypass the application.

A unique constraint protects alternate business identifiers such as a tenant-scoped external order number. Foreign keys do not automatically create supporting indexes in SQL Server, so inspect delete and join workloads. Cascading deletes need careful business review because one operation may remove a large related dataset.

Isolation levels trade concurrency against permitted anomalies. Read Uncommitted can observe uncommitted data; Read Committed prevents dirty reads, with locking or row-versioned implementation depending on configuration. Repeatable Read also protects rows read from modification, while Serializable protects relevant key ranges against phantoms.

Snapshot uses row versions for a transaction-consistent view and can encounter update conflicts. Read Committed Snapshot generally gives statement-level consistent reads. Choose isolation for the business invariant and measure contention. Row versioning reduces some reader/writer blocking but does not eliminate write conflicts, deadlocks or storage overhead.

A stored procedure packages server-side SQL with parameters and execution permissions. It can centralize data operations and reduce repeated network exchanges, but it is not inherently faster or immune to injection.

Review execution plans, parameter behavior and transaction scope just as for application queries. Parameterize dynamic SQL inside a procedure, and avoid giving callers broad database permissions. Version and test procedure changes alongside application deployments so older application instances remain compatible during rollout.

A view is a named query that presents a reusable relational interface over underlying tables. A normal view stores the query definition rather than a separate copy of its results. It can simplify access and hide selected columns.

Views do not automatically improve performance, and deeply nested views can obscure expensive joins. Indexed views materialize data under specific restrictions and add write-maintenance cost. Use views for a clear contract or demonstrated query need, and still inspect the final execution plan.
Pagination limits response size and database work. OFFSET/FETCH is simple for small offsets but can become expensive for deep pages because earlier rows must still be located and skipped.

Keyset pagination requests rows after the last ordered key, for example CreatedAt and OrderId. It needs a stable unique ordering and a matching index, and works well for next-page navigation. Use opaque continuation tokens, enforce maximum page size and explain how inserts or deletes between requests affect the user's view.

The client provider reuses physical database connections so each request avoids opening a new network session. Code should open late, close promptly and dispose reliably; disposal normally returns a connection to its pool.

A pool can be exhausted by leaked connections, long transactions, slow queries or excessive parallel work even when database CPU looks normal. Measure wait time and active connections, inspect reader disposal and compare distinct connection strings that create separate pools. Increasing the pool limit can shift overload to the database rather than fix it.

Batching combines multiple small operations to reduce round trips and per-operation overhead. Examples include fetching many related keys in one query or using a suitable bulk ingestion mechanism for large imports.

Choose a bounded batch size: one enormous transaction can consume memory and log space, hold locks and make recovery expensive. Record progress, support restart and enforce idempotency. Distinguish EF command batching from a true bulk-copy operation, and measure throughput together with lock time and failure recovery.

variants.wording: 19. How would you implement distributed caching using Redis in a .NET Core application?

sections.content: Use a supported Redis client or the distributed-cache abstraction, configured through DI. Cache serialized DTOs with explicit expiration and keys scoped by tenant, entity and representation version. Reuse the underlying connection infrastructure rather than creating a connection per request.

For cache-aside, read Redis first, load from the database on a miss and populate with a bounded TTL. Invalidate after writes and protect the origin from stampedes. IDistributedCache is a key/value abstraction; advanced atomic operations may require the Redis client directly.

Monitor latency, hit rate, evictions, connection errors and memory. Define a bounded fallback when Redis fails so the database is not suddenly flooded. Do not use a distributed cache as the sole durable payment or job record.

IMemoryCache stores typed objects in one application process and is lost when that process restarts; replicas have independent values. IDistributedCache exposes byte/string-oriented operations over a configured backing store shared by instances. Its interface alone does not guarantee remote storage: a distributed-memory implementation is still local to the process. Redis is one provider choice, with network and serialization costs.

A cache accelerates access to reusable data and may lose entries at any time. Session stores state associated with a user's interaction across requests, usually referenced by a session identifier. Neither should be the only durable record of a critical transaction.

In a scaled application, in-memory session can bind behavior to one instance. Use an appropriate distributed session store or redesign the flow around explicit durable state. Keep session small and consider its effects on concurrency, privacy and expiration.

Use caching for shared reference data, and session only for interaction state that truly needs it. Authentication cookies and tokens are separate mechanisms; enabling session does not authenticate the user.

Cache data that is expensive to compute or retrieve and can tolerate a defined period of staleness: reference data, product summaries or selected read models. Measure hit rate, response time, origin load and memory consumption to verify benefit.

Define the key, tenant/user scope, lifetime, invalidation owner and fallback behavior. A cache should usually be disposable and reconstructable from the source of truth. Avoid caching authorization decisions or personal data without precise isolation and invalidation rules.

An in-process cache is fastest but differs across instances. A distributed cache shares values at a network and serialization cost. Caching an inefficient query can hide a problem until a cold start or mass expiry overwhelms the database.

variants.wording: What happens when cached data becomes stale?

sections.content: Decide the acceptable staleness window before choosing a TTL. On a write, invalidate or refresh affected cache keys after the authoritative commit. Include tenant and representation/version information in keys to avoid serving the wrong data.

TTL provides a safety bound, while event-driven invalidation can reduce delay. Race conditions remain possible when a concurrent reader repopulates an old value; versioned keys, conditional updates or coordinated refresh may be necessary for sensitive workloads.

Prevent stampedes with single-flight loading, jittered expiry and bounded origin concurrency. Stale-while-revalidate is useful only when stale responses are acceptable. If strict current correctness is required, read the source of truth rather than promising perfect cache consistency.

With cache-aside, the application checks the cache, reads the database on a miss and populates the cache. Writes normally update the database and invalidate the cache. It is simple and fits read-heavy workloads, but miss storms and stale repopulation need attention.

With write-through, writes pass through a component that updates the backing store and cache as part of its defined behavior. This can keep frequently read values fresh, but adds latency and a difficult failure boundary; two separate systems are not automatically one atomic transaction.
Choose a pattern based on read/write ratios and consistency requirements. Document what happens when one write succeeds and the other fails, and always provide a way to rebuild the cache.

variants.wording: In React, explain useState vs useEffect and when useEffect runs.

sections.content: useState stores component state between renders. Updating it schedules a render; the setter does not immediately change the value captured by the current function call. Use a functional update when the next state depends on the previous state.

useEffect synchronizes a component with an external system after a committed render, such as subscribing to a connection. Without a dependency array it runs after every commit; with dependencies it reruns when they change under Object.is comparison. An empty array limits it to mounting for that component instance, with cleanup on unmount.

Cleanup runs before the next effect setup when dependencies change and on unmount. Development Strict Mode performs an additional setup/cleanup cycle to expose bugs. Effects are client-side and should not be used to calculate values that can be derived during rendering. Guard asynchronous responses against races and cancel obsolete work where possible.
Props are inputs supplied by a parent; state is data owned by a component or state container that can change over time. Both should be treated as immutable snapshots during rendering.

A child should request a change through a callback rather than mutate its props. Lift state to the nearest common owner when siblings must coordinate, and avoid copying a prop into state unless there is a clear synchronization requirement.

For a product form, the product ID may arrive as a prop while unsaved field edits are local state. Derived values such as the total should usually be calculated from existing data rather than stored separately and allowed to drift.

React renders a description of the desired UI and reconciles it with the previous render before committing necessary host changes to the real DOM. Component rendering does not imply that every corresponding browser element is recreated.

Stable keys help React associate list items across renders. Using an array index as a key for a reorderable list can attach state to the wrong item. Component type and position also affect identity and state preservation.

The virtual DOM is not a guarantee of speed. Expensive calculations, large trees, excessive subscriptions and browser layout work can still dominate. Measure render and commit behavior with profiling tools before adding memoization.

Hooks provide state, context, refs, effects and other React capabilities inside function components. Common examples include useState for state, useRef for a persistent mutable reference and useEffect for external synchronization.

Call Hooks at the top level of React components or custom Hooks, following the applicable Rules of Hooks. Conditional calls to ordinary state/effect Hooks change call order and break React's association between calls and stored state. Custom Hooks reuse behavior, not a single shared state instance by default.

Choose the hook according to the job: refs do not trigger renders, state does, and effects should not replace ordinary event handlers or render-time calculations. Keep dependency lists accurate to avoid stale closures.

useMemo caches a calculation result between renders when its dependencies remain unchanged. useCallback caches a function identity rather than its returned result. Both are performance tools, not requirements for correctness.

Use them when profiling shows an expensive calculation or when stable identity matters to a memoized child or subscription. Include every reactive dependency; omitting one can leave the cached value or callback using stale data.

Memoization has its own comparison and memory costs, and React may discard cached values in some circumstances. Do not depend on a cache for durable application state. A clear component design and local state placement often remove unnecessary rendering more effectively than wrapping everything in hooks.

variants.wording: 23️⃣ How would you optimize a slow React application?

sections.content: Measure whether the delay comes from network requests, JavaScript execution, React rendering or browser layout. Use the browser performance tools and React profiling to identify slow interactions and unnecessarily rerendered subtrees.

Reduce request waterfalls, cache server data appropriately, split large bundles and virtualize long lists. Keep rapidly changing state near its consumers, use stable list keys and avoid large context values that invalidate unrelated components. Apply memoization only where it removes measured work.

For search input, debounce requests when appropriate and cancel or ignore obsolete responses. Test on realistic devices and datasets, tracking interaction latency and loading experience. Optimizing render time will not fix an eight-second backend call.

questions.title: State in a large React application

variants.wording: 24️⃣ How would you manage state in a large application?

sections.content: Separate local UI state, shared client state, URL state and server state. Keep a modal's open flag local; put shareable filters in the URL; use a server-state cache for fetched records and invalidation; use context or a dedicated store for genuinely shared client behavior.

Define ownership and update paths so the same data is not duplicated across several stores. Reducers can make complex local transitions explicit, while selectors limit unrelated updates in a larger store.

Choose tooling based on concurrency, debugging and team needs. A global store for every input field increases coupling. Design loading, error, stale-data and optimistic-update behavior as part of the state model rather than adding it after the happy path.

variants.wording: 111. How would you implement Clean Architecture in a large-scale .NET application?
112. When would you choose Clean Architecture over traditional Layered Architecture?
5. How do you implement clean architecture, domain-driven design (DDD), SOLID principles, and design patterns in large enterprise applications?

sections.content: Clean Architecture places business rules in an inner domain layer, use cases in an application layer, and transport, persistence and external adapters at the edges. Compile-time dependencies point inward: an application use case depends on a persistence contract, and an infrastructure adapter implements it. The composition root wires them together.

In a large .NET system, define boundaries around business capabilities, keep EF and HTTP types out of core domain rules where practical, and test use cases without the web host. Dependency rules can be enforced with architecture tests. Avoid turning a simple operation into many meaningless wrappers.

Choose it when domain complexity, longevity and independently changing integrations justify the separation. Traditional layering is simpler for straightforward CRUD. Both approaches can be maintainable; the key distinction is dependency direction and protection of business rules, not the number of projects in the solution.

variants.wording: 113. How do you identify Bounded Contexts in a real-world .NET application using DDD?
118. How would you decide the boundaries of a Microservice?

sections.content: Start with business workflows, vocabulary, invariants and ownership. A Customer in billing may mean a legal payer, while Customer in support means a contact and entitlement record. Separate contexts where the same term has different rules or change drivers.

Use domain workshops and event mapping, inspect transaction dependencies and align ownership with teams. Define published contracts and an anti-corruption layer where one context translates another's model. A bounded context is a modeling boundary, not automatically one deployed microservice.

Prefer boundaries with high internal cohesion and limited synchronous chatter. Splitting by database table or technical layer often creates distributed joins and coupled releases. Validate a proposed boundary with actual use cases before moving code or data.

variants.wording: 114. How would you design Aggregate Roots and maintain consistency within an aggregate?

sections.content: An aggregate is a consistency boundary with a root that controls changes to its internal entities and value objects. For example, an Order root can enforce that a confirmed order cannot accept new lines and that its total matches its line items.

Keep aggregates small enough to load and update without excessive contention. Reference other aggregates by identity rather than requiring a giant object graph. Use optimistic concurrency and database constraints to protect concurrent updates.

Rules that must hold immediately should fit inside one transaction where possible. Cross-aggregate workflows often use events and eventual consistency, with explicitly modeled intermediate states and compensating actions. Do not place every related business object in one aggregate merely because it shares a foreign key.

variants.wording: 115. When would you choose a Modular Monolith instead of Microservices?

sections.content: A modular monolith packages well-defined business modules into one deployable application. It is often appropriate when one or a few teams need straightforward operations, shared release coordination and local transactions, while domain boundaries are still evolving.

Microservices can justify their operational cost when teams need independent deployment, materially different scaling or strong fault boundaries. They introduce network failures, distributed tracing, asynchronous consistency and contract-versioning work.

Choose based on organizational and workload needs. A modular monolith can later expose selected modules as services, provided its boundaries are enforced. A poorly separated monolith moved into containers is still tightly coupled, with additional network overhead.

variants.wording: 116. How would you prevent tight coupling between modules in a Modular Monolith?

sections.content: Give each module an explicit public contract and hide its implementation and persistence model. Other modules should use application APIs or published events, not reach into internal classes or update another module's tables directly.

Enforce references with project boundaries, internal visibility and architecture tests. Define data ownership even when modules share one physical database; separate schemas and permissions can strengthen the boundary.

Avoid a shared library that accumulates every entity and business rule. Share only stable technical utilities or carefully governed contracts. Measure cross-module calls and cyclic dependencies, because excessive synchronous interaction can reveal an incorrect business boundary.

variants.wording: 117. How would you migrate a large .NET Monolith to Microservices without disrupting production?

Q2. Your organisation plans to modernise a large .NET monolith into independently deployable services, but the application contains tightly coupled business logic and undocumented dependencies. How would you decide what to extract first, manage data ownership, and minimise disruption while continuing feature delivery?
Q10. You need to split a large .NET monolith into microservices. How would you decide the service boundaries and migrate safely?

sections.content: Map real dependencies before extraction: workflows, tables, scheduled jobs, reporting, integrations and production call paths. Use traces and domain workshops to expose undocumented coupling. Select a capability with clear ownership, meaningful value and manageable transaction dependencies rather than the largest or most fashionable component.

Use a strangler approach: route one capability to a new service behind a stable interface while the monolith continues operating. Establish a single authoritative writer for its data, backfill historical records and use a controlled change feed or events during transition. Avoid indefinite dual writes.

Use contract tests, reconciliation, feature flags, canary traffic and a rollback path. Continue feature delivery through small compatible changes. Track business correctness, latency and incident rate after each step. Extracting everything at once removes the opportunity to learn and makes failures harder to isolate.

variants.wording: 119. When should you use CQRS, and when can CQRS add unnecessary complexity?
96. CQRS — when does the added complexity actually pay off, and when have you talked a team out of using it?

sections.content: CQRS separates models or paths for commands that change state and queries that read it. It does not inherently require separate databases, asynchronous messaging or event sourcing. A simple implementation can use the same database with different write and read services.

It pays off when write invariants differ substantially from read projections, read scaling is highly asymmetric or complex reporting should not distort the write model. Separate read stores introduce lag, rebuilding, event handling and operational complexity.

For simple CRUD with similar read/write shapes, I would recommend ordinary application services and projections. For the interview's personal follow-up about persuading a team, describe a real decision if you have one; otherwise present this as a hypothetical tradeoff analysis, not an experience you have not had.

questions.title: Order payment inventory and shipping events

variants.wording: 120. How would you implement Event-Driven Architecture for Order, Payment, Inventory and Shipping services?

sections.content: An order workflow can start with OrderSubmitted, reserve inventory, authorize payment and then request shipment. Each service owns its data and publishes facts after local state commits. Define contracts with event IDs, entity IDs, version, timestamp and correlation information.

Use an outbox for reliable publication and idempotent consumers for redelivery. Model intermediate states such as PendingPayment and AwaitingInventory rather than pretending the entire flow is one atomic transaction. A workflow coordinator can make timeouts and compensation easier to see.

If payment fails, release reserved inventory; if a later step fails, decide whether to retry, refund or escalate. Event ordering and duplicate delivery must be explicit. Monitor workflow age and stuck states, not only the success of individual message handlers.

variants.wording: 121. How would you handle distributed transactions across multiple Microservices using the Saga Pattern?

sections.content: A saga coordinates a business transaction through local transactions in separate services. Each successful step has a business compensation where reversal is possible. An orchestrator sends commands and tracks state; choreography lets services react to events without a central coordinator.

For an order, reserve inventory, authorize payment and schedule shipping. A payment failure triggers inventory release. Compensation is a new business operation, not a database rollback, and some actions such as a shipped parcel cannot be undone automatically.

Persist saga state, use idempotent commands and handlers, define timeouts and handle late messages. Include manual intervention for irrecoverable cases. Sagas trade immediate global consistency for explicit recovery and availability; they are unnecessary when one local transaction can satisfy the requirement.

variants.wording: 122. What problem does the Outbox Pattern solve, and how would you implement it in .NET?

sections.content: The outbox solves the dual-write gap between committing database changes and publishing a message. If the commit succeeds but publication fails, downstream systems may never learn about the change; publishing first can announce a change that later rolls back.

Save the business update and an outbox event in one local database transaction. A background publisher reads pending records, sends them to the broker and marks them published. Use event IDs, safe claiming between workers and retry monitoring.

A crash after send but before marking produces a duplicate publication, so consumers must still be idempotent. Outbox provides reliable eventual publication, not magical exactly-once end-to-end execution. Retain records long enough for troubleshooting and clean them up with a defined policy.

questions.title: Idempotent message processing

variants.wording: 123. How would you design an idempotent Microservice that can safely process duplicate messages?
5. Idempotency with Service Bus and Azure Functions

sections.content: At-least-once delivery means a handler may receive the same message repeatedly. Give each event a stable ID and enforce a unique processed-message key per consumer. In one local transaction, record the ID and apply the business change; a duplicate then becomes a safe no-op.

Complete the broker message only after durable processing succeeds. If the process crashes before acknowledgment, redelivery is expected. For remote side effects, pass a stable idempotency key to the downstream system or model an outbox/workflow with reconciliation.

Broker duplicate detection helps within its configured scope and time window but cannot replace business idempotency. Azure Functions scaling makes races more likely, so do not use only an in-memory set or a check-then-insert without a uniqueness constraint.

references: Further reading: Service Bus message loss and duplicates

variants.wording: 124. When would you use Azure Service Bus Queue vs Topic/Subscription?

sections.content: A queue buffers work for competing consumers: one message is normally processed by one consumer, subject to redelivery. A Service Bus topic fans messages out to subscriptions so independent consumers such as billing and analytics can each process their own copy.

Messaging decouples availability and absorbs bursts, but adds eventual consistency, duplicate handling and operational monitoring. Use a queue for a single processing responsibility and topic subscriptions for independent reactions to the same event.

Define message contracts, retention, failure handling and ordering requirements. Sessions can support ordered processing for a logical stream when needed. Do not assume a globally ordered queue or unlimited buffering will solve an overloaded downstream database.

questions.title: Retries and dead letter queues

variants.wording: 125. How would you handle message failures, retries and Dead-Letter Queues in Azure Service Bus?

sections.content: Classify failures before retrying. Transient network or service failures may recover; malformed payloads, invalid business data and authorization errors usually need correction. Apply bounded retries with backoff and jitter and avoid overlapping retry loops at every layer.

Use a dead-letter queue for messages that cannot be processed after policy limits or are deliberately rejected. Record the reason, event ID and correlation ID without leaking secrets. Alert on count, age and growth so the DLQ does not become a silent archive.

Build a controlled replay process after fixing the cause, preserving idempotency and ordering where required. A broker can redeliver after lock expiration, so tune processing duration and lock renewal appropriately. Retrying forever consumes resources and hides poison messages.

references: Further reading: Service Bus dead letter queues

variants.wording: 98. If you just centralize object creation, is that the Factory Pattern?
99. What is the difference between Factory Method and Factory Pattern?

sections.content: Centralizing object creation is often called a simple factory, especially when a method chooses among concrete implementations. The broad term Factory Pattern is ambiguous; clarify which variant the interviewer means.

Factory Method is a specific pattern where a creator exposes a construction method that derived types override to choose a product. A static switch-based factory is not automatically that pattern. Dependency injection registration also centralizes construction, but its primary purpose is composing object dependencies and lifetimes.
Use a factory when construction depends on runtime input or involves a meaningful creation policy. Avoid a factory that merely calls new for a trivial type without isolating variation or complexity.

variants.wording: 100. What is the Abstract Factory Pattern? Explain with a real-time example.

sections.content: Abstract Factory creates a family of related products through one contract. For a document export application, an IReportComponentFactory might create a renderer, stylesheet provider and asset encoder. A PDF family and an HTML family provide compatible components.

The client depends on the family interfaces, while a composition root selects the concrete factory. This prevents accidentally combining a PDF renderer with HTML-only assets. It differs from Factory Method, which focuses on overridable creation of an individual product.
Use it when multiple products must vary together. If only one service differs, a strategy or simple factory is often easier to understand and test.

variants.wording: 104. Explain the SOLID Principles. Why do we use them in real-world applications?
5️⃣ Explain SOLID with a project example.

sections.content: Single Responsibility means a component has one coherent reason to change: order pricing should not also send email and format invoices. Open/Closed favors adding a pricing strategy rather than editing a growing conditional for every customer. Liskov Substitution requires replacements to preserve the promised behavior.

Interface Segregation gives callers focused contracts, such as reading inventory separately from administering it. Dependency Inversion makes high-level checkout logic depend on a payment abstraction, with provider adapters outside the core.

In a checkout project, inject IPricingPolicy and IPaymentGateway into an application service and keep persistence at a boundary. These principles improve testability and change isolation, but do not require one interface per class. Judge the design by how safely it accommodates real changes, not by how many patterns it contains.

variants.wording: 3. How do you design scalable, secure, and high-performance microservices architectures using ASP.NET Core, Docker, Kubernetes, and cloud platforms?

sections.content: Start with business boundaries and data ownership, then choose independent deployment units where team autonomy or workload demands justify them. Each service owns its persistence and publishes a stable API or event contract; other services do not write its tables.

Use synchronous calls for immediate results and messaging for durable asynchronous workflows. Apply outbox, idempotency and sagas where needed, along with timeouts, bounded concurrency and contract tests. Secure external and internal access using workload identity and resource-level authorization.

Containerize reproducibly and use Kubernetes only when its orchestration capabilities justify the operational investment. Add traces, metrics, logs, health checks and progressive rollout. Test database limits and failure propagation because more replicas cannot compensate for a shared bottleneck or a poorly chosen boundary.

questions.title: Retries circuit breakers and failure handling

variants.wording: Q2. Your application needs to call an external API that sometimes fails or responds slowly. How would you make the integration resilient?

sections.content: Set a total operation deadline and smaller per-attempt timeouts. Retry only transient failures and only when the operation is safe to repeat. Use exponential backoff with jitter, respect Retry-After and avoid retrying validation or authorization failures.

A circuit breaker temporarily stops calls after a failure threshold so an unhealthy dependency can recover. It does not retry a request; it limits further attempts. Bulkheads or bounded concurrency prevent one dependency from exhausting all application resources.

In .NET, configure HttpClient and an appropriate resilience handler deliberately, propagate cancellation and trace attempts. Cache or degrade responses only when the business accepts stale or partial data. Test timeouts, partial success and recovery, especially when a POST may have succeeded before the connection failed.

Use synchronous HTTP or gRPC when the caller needs an immediate result and the dependency chain is acceptably short. Use asynchronous messages for durable work, independent subscribers or workflows that can tolerate delayed completion.

Every network boundary needs timeouts, cancellation, authentication, versioned contracts and telemetry. For messages, add idempotency, schema evolution and replay strategy. For synchronous calls, bound concurrency and prevent cascading retries.

Avoid long chains of synchronous calls for one user request. A read model or coarse-grained API may reduce chatty coordination. Choose communication based on business latency and consistency requirements rather than a rule that microservices must communicate only through events.

A repository provides a domain-oriented persistence boundary, such as loading an Order aggregate and saving its changes. It can isolate persistence details and offer a focused testing seam. EF Core's DbContext and DbSet already provide much repository and unit-of-work behavior.

Add a custom repository when it expresses domain operations or protects an aggregate boundary. Avoid a generic CRUD wrapper that merely forwards every EF method and makes projection, batching or transactions harder. Returning unrestricted IQueryable can leak persistence concerns to consumers; choose that tradeoff consciously rather than claiming complete abstraction.

variants.wording: 126. When would you choose Azure Functions instead of an ASP.NET Core Web API?

sections.content: Azure Functions suits event-triggered units of work, scheduled tasks and integrations that benefit from managed trigger bindings and elastic execution. ASP.NET Core Web API suits a richer HTTP application with extensive middleware, routing, domain orchestration and control over hosting behavior.

Consider execution duration, response-time predictability, traffic shape, deployment model and dependencies. A long-running workflow may need durable orchestration or a queued worker regardless of how the HTTP entry point is hosted.

Use the simplest operational model that meets the requirement. Functions are not automatically cheaper, and APIs can also scale elastically. Avoid hiding a whole tightly coupled application inside one enormous function.

variants.wording: 129. How would you design Azure API Management for a Microservices-based .NET application?

sections.content: Place APIM at the external API boundary to provide a consistent contract, authentication checks, quotas, routing and observability. Organize APIs and products around consumers and business capabilities, with versioning and environment-specific backends.

Validate tokens and apply appropriate rate limits, but retain resource-level authorization in services. Use managed identity or another secure backend authentication method, restrict direct backend exposure where required and propagate trace context.

Keep policies focused on gateway concerns rather than complex business workflows. Treat policy and API definition changes as reviewed deployments, and capacity-plan the gateway itself. APIM cannot make an unhealthy backend reliable simply by retrying requests.

variants.wording: 130. How would you design a highly scalable .NET + Azure architecture using APIM, Service Bus, Functions, Blob Storage, Key Vault and Azure SQL?

sections.content: Use APIM as the HTTP entry point, with an ASP.NET Core application handling authorization and short synchronous operations. Store transactional data in Azure SQL and large documents in Blob Storage. Persist an outbox event with the business change, then publish to Service Bus.

Functions or worker services consume messages using bounded concurrency and idempotent processing. Use queues for work distribution and topic subscriptions for independent integrations. Store secrets in Key Vault and prefer managed identities for service access.

Design for failure with DLQs, retries, status endpoints and reconciliation. Apply private connectivity where required, define backup and regional recovery objectives, and monitor end-to-end latency and queue age. Scale each component against measured demand without exceeding database or external-system limits.

variants.wording: 6. Describe your experience with Azure, CI/CD pipelines, DevOps practices, Infrastructure as Code, and cloud-native application development.

sections.content: A reliable pipeline builds a reproducible artifact, runs focused tests and security checks, and promotes the same artifact through environments. Keep configuration outside the binary and provision infrastructure from reviewed code.

Use short-lived deployment credentials or workload identity, least privilege and environment controls appropriate to risk. Deploy with health checks, progressive exposure and a rollback or forward-fix plan. Database changes must remain compatible with overlapping application versions.

From the supplied resume, Azure DevOps and CI/CD are supported experience areas. Explain a real pipeline you owned, its quality gates and a measurable delivery improvement. Do not claim Kubernetes or Terraform production ownership unless that matches your actual work.

questions.title: Logic Apps Consumption and Standard

sections.content: Consumption uses the multitenant service and is attractive for intermittent integration workloads with consumption-based execution billing. Standard uses the single-tenant runtime, supports multiple workflows in one resource and offers hosting and networking options useful for enterprise integration.

Choose based on connector support, stateful versus stateless needs, throughput, network isolation, deployment practices and total cost. Standard can offer more predictable dedicated capacity, but idle capacity and connector charges must be included in the comparison.

Prototype the actual workflow and verify regional, plan and connector capabilities. A workflow that is cheap at low volume may become expensive with many actions, while a dedicated plan may be wasteful for rare runs. Service capabilities evolve, so validate the selected hosting plan before committing.

references: Further reading: Logic Apps hosting comparison

variants.wording: 2. Scaling Azure Functions under high load

sections.content: Understand the hosting plan and trigger because they determine scaling behavior and available controls. Queue depth, event arrival and concurrency can drive more workers, but additional instances do not increase a downstream database's capacity.

Measure execution duration, queue age, failures and dependency saturation. Set bounded concurrency, use efficient async I/O and reuse clients. Partition work appropriately and avoid one hot key or session serializing the entire workload.

Load-test realistic bursts and recovery after an outage. Plan for service quotas, retries, idempotency and poison messages. Scaling settings, minimum instances and networking options vary by plan; select them from current documentation rather than assuming every Function App scales identically.

A cold start is the delay while an inactive or new worker initializes the host and application before serving work. Dependency loading, startup code, network initialization and package size can contribute.

Reduce unnecessary startup work and large dependency graphs, initialize clients appropriately and measure cold and warm latency separately. Choose a hosting option with prewarmed or always-ready capacity when the latency objective justifies its cost.

Do not promise zero startup delay merely because a plan reduces cold starts: deployment, scaling and failures can still create new workers. For latency-critical user requests, compare a continuously running API with a function-based design using measured workload behavior.

variants.wording: 4. Migrating Logic Apps from Consumption to Standard

sections.content: Inventory workflows, triggers, connectors, identities, network dependencies, run history requirements and external callbacks. Check which actions and connector behaviors transfer directly and which require redesign in the target hosting model.

Provision the Standard environment and connection configuration through a repeatable deployment process. Test stateful behavior, concurrency, retries, network access and throughput with realistic payloads. Recreate permissions and secrets through managed configuration rather than copying credentials casually.

Cut over with a controlled trigger handoff so two workflows do not process the same events unexpectedly. Preserve checkpoints and define rollback and reconciliation. Migration is not only exporting JSON: runtime, networking, billing and operational behavior must all be validated.

variants.wording: 7. VNet Integration in Logic Apps Standard

sections.content: VNet integration supports outbound connectivity from the application to resources reachable through the virtual network. Private endpoints control private inbound access to supported services; the two concepts solve different directions of connectivity.

Plan subnet requirements, routing, DNS, firewall rules and access to storage and connectors. A private hostname resolving to a public address can break the intended isolation even when the subnet configuration appears correct.

Test from the application's effective network path, including all required service endpoints and managed connectors. Document which traffic remains on public managed infrastructure. Avoid saying that enabling VNet integration automatically makes every inbound endpoint private.

Bicep is an Azure-focused declarative language that compiles to ARM templates and fits closely with Azure resource deployment. Terraform uses providers to manage many platforms and tracks managed resources in state.

Choose Bicep for Azure-native simplicity and integration when that aligns with team practice. Choose Terraform when its provider ecosystem, existing modules and cross-platform consistency offer material value. Neither choice eliminates the need for good module boundaries and deployment review.

Secure state and deployment identities, pin dependencies, review planned changes and detect drift. Avoid managing the same resource through both tools. An interview answer should describe a real deployment example only if you have used the chosen tool; otherwise present the design as your proposed approach.

variants.wording: 9. Designing event-driven solutions for millions of records

sections.content: Separate ingestion from processing with durable storage and messaging. Store large payloads in Blob Storage and send small references, record IDs and schema versions through the broker. Partition work so workers can process independently without one global lock.

Use bounded batches, idempotent writes and checkpoints so processing can resume after failure. Apply backpressure based on database and downstream capacity rather than maximizing worker count. Choose partition keys that distribute load while preserving required ordering.

Measure throughput, oldest-message age, failure rate and cost per record. Test replay, duplicate delivery and partial batch failure. A successful load test includes recovery from backlog and downstream throttling, not only a short burst at peak speed.

Isolate each downstream system behind an adapter with a clear contract, authentication method, timeout and error mapping. For asynchronous fan-out, independent subscriptions prevent a slow consumer from blocking unrelated integrations.

Track delivery state per destination, use stable idempotency keys and define whether partial completion is acceptable. A workflow may need compensation or manual reconciliation when one system accepts a change and another rejects it.

Version canonical events carefully and avoid a single giant shared model that mirrors every destination. Monitor per-system latency, failures and backlog, with bounded retries and a repair process. Do not assume a successful upstream response means every downstream system has completed.

Determine whether the trigger is firing, the host is healthy and the function code starts. Review invocation IDs, Application Insights traces, exceptions and dependency calls. For missing events, inspect trigger configuration, connection permissions, checkpoints and broker backlog.

For failed executions, distinguish code defects from timeouts, memory pressure, scaling limits, lock expiration and downstream throttling. Check deployment configuration, runtime compatibility, identity and network changes, even when the function code has not changed.

Use a representative event in a safe environment and compare healthy and failing instances. Preserve failed messages for replay, fix the root cause and validate idempotency before reprocessing. Avoid repeated restarts that destroy useful diagnostic context.

questions.title: Backend works directly but APIM returns 502

variants.wording: 11. APIM troubleshooting, including why a backend can work directly but still return 502 through APIM

sections.content: A direct test proves only that the backend works from that caller's network and with that request. Capture APIM gateway diagnostics or a trace and determine whether the failure occurs before connecting, during TLS, while sending the request or while reading the response.

Compare the effective backend URL, rewritten path, host header, port, credentials, certificate chain and timeout. Check DNS and routing from APIM's network, private endpoints, firewall rules and backend allowlists. Review policies that change headers, bodies or routing.

Correlate gateway and backend timestamps: no backend request suggests connectivity or policy failure; a recorded backend request may reveal a timeout or malformed response. Reproduce with the same method and payload and avoid disabling certificate validation as a permanent workaround.

variants.wording: 12. Designing highly available and disaster recovery-ready solutions

sections.content: Define business RTO, the acceptable recovery time, and RPO, the acceptable data loss, before choosing architecture. High availability handles expected local failures; disaster recovery restores service after a larger outage such as regional loss.

Use zone-resilient components where supported, database backup/replication, repeatable infrastructure deployment and a documented traffic failover process. Include identities, secrets, DNS, messaging state, search indexes and third-party dependencies in the plan.

Run recovery exercises that restore data and execute a real business workflow. Monitor replication lag and validate backups. Active-active designs add conflict and consistency complexity; choose them only when recovery objectives justify the operational burden.

A load balancer distributes requests across healthy application instances. Readiness checks, connection behavior and the balancing algorithm affect how evenly work is spread. Removing an instance from routing should precede termination so in-flight requests can drain.

Keep application state external or explicitly manage session affinity where unavoidable. Autoscaling adds or removes capacity, while load balancing distributes traffic; they are related but different functions.

Monitor per-instance latency and resource use because an even request count may still produce uneven work. Ensure the shared database and other dependencies can support aggregate traffic, and test failover rather than only steady-state throughput.

A CDN caches eligible content near users to reduce origin traffic and network distance. Static frontend assets with content-hashed filenames are a good fit because they can have long lifetimes without serving the wrong version.

Define cache keys, headers, invalidation and origin protection. Be especially careful with authenticated or tenant-specific responses so one user's content is never reused for another. Not every API response should be cached at the edge.
Measure hit ratio and real user latency, and plan deployment behavior when HTML and asset versions differ. A CDN can accelerate delivery but cannot repair a slow uncached database operation.

Docker packages an application and its runtime dependencies into an image that runs as a container. Containers share the host kernel rather than carrying a full guest operating system, which makes them different from virtual machines.

For .NET, use a multi-stage build, a suitable runtime image, a non-root process where practical and explicit configuration. Keep secrets out of image layers, scan dependencies and send logs to standard output.

Containers improve packaging consistency but do not supply availability, persistent storage or secure configuration automatically. Define health checks, resource limits and graceful shutdown, and rebuild images to receive underlying security updates.

Kubernetes orchestrates containers using declarative desired state. Deployments manage replicas and rollout, Services provide stable discovery, and probes help identify readiness and liveness. Resource requests and limits influence scheduling and isolation.

For a .NET API, design graceful shutdown, externalize state and configure autoscaling from useful workload signals. Distinguish readiness failures that stop traffic from liveness failures that restart the process; an overly aggressive liveness probe can worsen an outage.

Kubernetes adds operational complexity involving networking, policies, upgrades and observability. Use it when workload and organizational requirements justify that platform, rather than assuming every microservice needs a cluster.

questions.title: Securing React and ASP NET Core

variants.wording: How would you secure a React + ASP.NET Core API using JWT/OAuth?
7. How do you ensure application security, compliance, authentication, authorization, and data protection in enterprise-grade .NET solutions?
🔟 How would you secure a production REST API?

sections.content: Use an established OpenID Connect provider for sign-in and issue audience-specific access tokens. For a React SPA, Authorization Code with PKCE is appropriate; a backend-for-frontend with secure HttpOnly cookies is another option that reduces token exposure to browser scripts. Cookie-based designs need CSRF protection.

At the API, validate tokens, enforce policies and tenant/resource ownership, validate input and parameterize database access. Apply HTTPS, restrictive CORS, rate and payload limits, safe error responses and secret-free structured logging. CORS is a browser access policy, not authentication.

Protect secrets with managed identity and a vault, encrypt sensitive data as required, limit retention and audit privileged operations. Secure the delivery pipeline with dependency scanning and least privilege. Threat-model actual flows, including file uploads and AI/tool access, rather than treating JWT installation as complete security.

variants.wording: 127. How would you securely manage connection strings, API keys and secrets using Azure Key Vault?
95. Explain your approach to Secrets Rotation and Managed Identity across a large microservices estate.

sections.content: First reduce secrets by using managed identities wherever the target supports them. For remaining credentials, keep an inventory with owners, permissions, expiry, rotation procedures and dependency mappings. Store secrets in Key Vault, not source code or deployment logs.

Rotate through overlapping valid credentials where possible: create the replacement, update consumers, verify adoption and then revoke the old value. Account for application caches and long-lived connections; changing a vault value does not guarantee every running process immediately uses it.

Automate rotation and test it in lower environments and controlled production exercises. Alert on expiry and access anomalies, maintain a documented emergency process and scope each workload's access. A shared high-privilege credential across all microservices makes both rotation and incident containment harder.

variants.wording: 128. How would you use Managed Identity with Azure Key Vault in a .NET application?
6. Managed Identity and System Assigned vs User Assigned

sections.content: A managed identity gives an Azure workload an identity whose credentials are managed by the platform. Grant that identity the minimum target-service permissions, and let an Azure SDK credential acquire tokens rather than reading a stored client secret.

A system-assigned identity is tied to one resource's lifecycle. A user-assigned identity is independently managed and can be attached to supported resources, making permissions more stable across replacements; sharing it too widely increases blast radius.

For Key Vault, enable the identity, assign the appropriate data-plane role and use SecretClient with the intended credential. Distinguish local developer credentials from production identity selection, and verify both network access and permissions when troubleshooting a 403 or connectivity failure.

variants.wording: Q3. A critical security vulnerability is discovered in a third-party .NET dependency days before a major production release. Replacing the dependency could delay the release, while proceeding creates security exposure. What factors would you evaluate before recommending whether to patch, replace, isolate, or postpone the affected functionality?

sections.content: Establish the affected versions, exploit prerequisites, whether the vulnerable path is reachable and whether exploitation is known. Assess internet exposure, privilege, data sensitivity and available compensating controls. A severity score is useful context, but reachability and impact drive the release decision.

Prefer a supported patch with focused regression and integration tests. If replacement is costly, evaluate disabling the affected feature or isolating access as a temporary measure with a named owner and expiry. Validate that the mitigation actually blocks the exploit path.

Recommend postponement when a material exploitable risk cannot be reduced acceptably. Present security, delivery and operational tradeoffs to the accountable decision makers, document the decision and monitor until remediation is complete. Do not silently accept exposure to preserve a date or claim isolation without evidence.

variants.wording: 6. Authentication vs Authorization — what actually happens when a JWT request reaches an API?

sections.content: Authentication establishes the caller's identity; authorization decides whether that identity can perform the requested action on the particular resource. A valid JWT proves only that the token passed validation, not that its holder can access every tenant or record.

The bearer handler validates the token and builds a ClaimsPrincipal. Authorization then evaluates endpoint metadata and policies. Missing or invalid credentials typically lead to 401; a valid authenticated identity without permission typically receives 403.

Check ownership and tenant boundaries within the resource operation, not only at the controller attribute. A role named User is insufficient to authorize access to another customer's invoice. Claims used for decisions must come from a trusted validated identity.

questions.title: JWT flow

variants.wording: 7. Explain JWT authentication flow in ASP.NET Core from token generation to [Authorize].

sections.content: A trusted authorization server authenticates the user and issues an access token for the API. The client sends it in the Authorization Bearer header over HTTPS. JWT is a token format, not a login protocol, and its payload is normally readable rather than encrypted.

ASP.NET Core's bearer handler validates the signature, issuer, audience and lifetime using trusted configuration and signing keys. It creates a principal, then authorization middleware and policies enforce endpoint requirements such as [Authorize].

Use an established identity provider rather than casually building a token issuer. Support signing-key rotation, short token lifetimes and a clear revocation strategy. Decoding a token without validating it provides no security, and an ID token intended for a client must not be substituted for an API access token.

references: Further reading: Configure JWT bearer authentication

sections.content: CORS tells a browser which origins may read cross-origin responses. Configure explicit trusted origins, methods and headers, and account for preflight requests. Server-to-server clients are not constrained by browser CORS enforcement.

Do not combine a wildcard origin with credentials. When diagnosing a failure, distinguish a rejected preflight from an API authentication failure or a network error. CORS does not prevent a malicious client from calling the API and does not replace authorization or CSRF defenses.

SQL injection occurs when untrusted input changes the structure of executable SQL. Use parameterized commands or properly translated EF queries so input is treated as data. Stored procedures are vulnerable too if they concatenate unsafe dynamic SQL.

Parameters generally represent values, not arbitrary identifiers. For selectable columns or sort directions, use an allowlist and build only known-safe syntax. Apply least-privilege database permissions and avoid exposing database error details. Input validation helps business correctness but does not replace parameterization.

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework for delegated access to resources. OpenID Connect adds an identity layer for user sign-in. Neither is synonymous with JWT: access tokens can have different formats.

For a browser application, use an established provider and Authorization Code with PKCE. A public browser client cannot safely hold a client secret. For machine-to-machine access, use an appropriate workload identity or confidential-client flow.

Validate access tokens at the resource API and request the minimum scopes. Distinguish delegated user permissions from application permissions so a background process does not inadvertently gain authority intended only for an interactive user.
HTTPS uses TLS to protect confidentiality and integrity in transit and authenticate the server through certificates. It does not make application authorization or stored data secure by itself.

Terminate TLS at a trusted edge or application endpoint and secure the onward connection according to the threat model. Configure certificate renewal, modern protocols and trusted proxy headers. Use HSTS where appropriate, but remember that redirecting an HTTP request cannot undo sensitive data already sent in plaintext.

In general, hashing maps input to a fixed-size digest. Cryptographic hashes aim to resist reversing the digest and finding collisions, while ordinary collection hash codes serve a different purpose and are not security primitives.

Store passwords using a vetted adaptive password-hashing implementation rather than encryption or a fast general-purpose hash. A unique random salt prevents equal passwords from producing equal stored hashes and defeats precomputed lookup tables; the work factor makes guessing expensive.

Use an established identity system with upgradeable hashing settings, account protections and MFA support. Do not invent a custom algorithm or log passwords. Encryption is reversible with a key and is suitable for data that must be recovered; password verification normally needs a one-way check, not recovery.

Role checks are simple authorization conditions, while policies combine requirements such as scope, role, tenant membership or resource ownership. Custom authorization handlers can evaluate business-specific rules using trusted claims and the requested resource.

Keep policies named around capabilities, such as CanApproveInvoice, rather than scattering string checks across controllers. Resource-level checks remain necessary even when a user has the correct role. Test both allowed and denied cases, including cross-tenant IDs and expired or wrong-audience tokens.

A refresh token allows a client to request new access tokens without repeating the interactive sign-in. It is a high-value credential and must be protected, limited to its intended client and revocable.

Use the identity provider's supported rotation and reuse-detection behavior, define absolute and idle expiration, and revoke on relevant account events. Browser storage choices require an XSS/CSRF threat assessment; long-lived tokens in localStorage are accessible to injected scripts. Do not send refresh tokens to ordinary resource APIs.

variants.wording: What is Azure AI Search, and why would you use it in an AI application?

sections.content: Azure AI Search is a managed indexing and retrieval service that supports text search and vector-based retrieval, with filtering and relevance features. In an AI application, it can locate the enterprise passages supplied to an LLM as grounding context.

Build an ingestion pipeline that extracts content, splits it into useful chunks and indexes text, vectors and metadata such as source, version and access scope. Keep the index synchronized with source changes and deletions.

The search index is not the LLM and does not itself guarantee a correct answer. Retrieval quality, document permissions and freshness determine whether the model receives useful evidence. Apply access filters before content enters the prompt.

questions.title: RAG end to end

sections.content: Retrieval-augmented generation combines search over external knowledge with an LLM response. Offline, collect permitted documents, extract text, clean and chunk it, create embeddings and index chunks with source IDs and access metadata.

At query time, authenticate the user, determine allowed scope, retrieve relevant chunks using text/vector or hybrid search, optionally rerank, and build a prompt containing the question and evidence. Ask the model to answer from the evidence and include citations. Return an explicit insufficient-evidence response when necessary.

Evaluate retrieval and generation separately using representative questions with expected sources and answers. Monitor cost, latency, freshness and groundedness. Treat retrieved instructions as untrusted content, prevent cross-tenant retrieval and restrict tool access. RAG improves access to current knowledge but does not eliminate hallucinations.

references: Further reading: RAG with Azure AI Search

variants.wording: Embeddings vs Vector Search vs Hybrid Search — explain the difference.

sections.content: An embedding is a numeric representation produced by a model so related content tends to have related vectors. Indexing and querying must use compatible embedding spaces; equal dimensions alone do not make two models interchangeable.

Vector search ranks stored vectors by a similarity measure and can find semantically related passages even when wording differs. Keyword search is valuable for exact identifiers, product codes and specialized terms that semantic similarity may blur.

Hybrid search combines lexical and vector retrieval, typically fusing ranked candidates and optionally reranking. It can improve coverage, but requires evaluation of filters, candidate counts and chunk quality. Embeddings are representations, vector search is a retrieval method, and hybrid search combines retrieval methods.

variants.wording: Your RAG application is giving irrelevant answers. How would you troubleshoot it?

sections.content: Start with a failing question and inspect the actual retrieved chunks before changing the prompt. Verify tenant/security filters, index freshness, document extraction, chunk boundaries and embedding-model compatibility. Check whether the expected document was indexed at all.

If the correct content is absent from candidates, improve retrieval using query rewriting, hybrid search, metadata filters or better chunking. If it is present but ranked poorly, evaluate ranking and reranking. Tune top-k against an evaluation set rather than increasing it until irrelevant context dominates.

If evidence is good but the answer is wrong, inspect prompt instructions, context truncation, citation mapping and model behavior. Measure retrieval recall and answer groundedness separately. Include abstention tests and adversarial retrieved content, and compare changes against a fixed baseline before deploying.

variants.wording: Azure OpenAI/LLM is returning 429 Too Many Requests. How would you handle it?

sections.content: Inspect the 429 response and service metrics to distinguish request-rate, token-rate and capacity constraints. Large prompts and high maximum output allowances can consume quota rapidly even at modest request counts.

Respect Retry-After when supplied and use bounded exponential backoff with jitter within a total deadline. Limit concurrent requests, queue noninteractive work and reduce unnecessary tokens. Track retries so they do not amplify an overload.

For sustained demand, adjust capacity or deployment distribution within supported quota and policy constraints. Cache safe repeat responses where appropriate and provide a clear busy response or fallback. Do not retry indefinitely or assume that creating more application instances increases model-service quota.

questions.title: NET React Azure and RAG architecture

variants.wording: Design a scalable .NET + React + Azure + RAG application. Explain the architecture.

sections.content: Use React for the interface, an identity provider for sign-in and APIM plus ASP.NET Core for the application boundary. Enforce tenant and resource authorization in the API. Keep transactional records in Azure SQL or a suitable domain store, documents in Blob Storage and frequently reused safe data in a distributed cache.

A durable ingestion pipeline uses messaging and workers to extract, validate, chunk and index documents in Azure AI Search. The query path authenticates the user, applies access filters, retrieves evidence and calls the model through a controlled AI integration layer. Stream responses only when the client and error contract support it.

Use managed identities, Key Vault for remaining secrets, trace IDs across retrieval and generation, and explicit model quotas. Scale API, ingestion and model concurrency independently. Test cross-tenant isolation, grounding, prompt injection, queue replay and regional recovery. Measure latency, quality and cost together rather than optimizing only requests per second.

variants.wording: Have you ever implemented AI projects in your .net projects.
1. How have you leveraged AI, Generative AI, GitHub Copilot, Azure AI Services, or LLMs within .NET applications to improve business outcomes?

sections.content: Resume-grounded draft: I have worked on enterprise AI integration in a .NET and Azure environment, including an AI Email Dashboard that translates natural-language requests into parameterized, tenant-scoped SQL through an OpenAI-compatible gateway. The design includes claim-based tenant isolation, RBAC and guardrails, with MCP resources for schema, tenant metadata and conversation history.

Explain the business workflow first, then your own contribution: how requests were validated, what data the model could access, how generated actions were constrained and how failures were observed. Your additional confirmed Python experience is one year building production APIs and data pipelines; it should not be presented as expert-level Python experience.

Your resume lists broader efficiency and savings achievements, but attach a number to this specific project only if you can substantiate that connection. For Copilot, Azure AI Services or other named tools in the question, state actual usage and measured outcome; do not imply that every listed tool was used simply because the interviewer mentioned it.

variants.wording: Explain Current Project Architecture , Roles & Responsibilities.
2. Describe the most complex enterprise application or modernization project you have delivered using .NET, .NET Core/.NET 8+, and cloud technologies.

sections.content: Resume-grounded outline: describe the enterprise compliance platform you support as a Technical Lead, with an Angular/PrimeNG front end, .NET APIs, Azure services and SQL Server/Cosmos DB persistence. Explain where Dapper, Azure Functions and CI/CD fit only to the extent they match the specific project you choose.

Walk through one request: authentication and tenant context, API validation, application/domain rules, persistence, integration and telemetry. Explain security boundaries and a design decision you personally influenced. For modernization, describe the starting limitation, migration steps and compatibility strategy.

Separate your individual responsibilities from the team's work: architecture, implementation, code review, mentoring, release delivery and production support. Use resume metrics only with the correct scope and evidence. Do not combine every employer's technologies into a fictional single application or claim an end-to-end project you did not own.

questions.title: Latency and failures after a release

variants.wording: Q1. A high-traffic .NET application begins experiencing severe latency and intermittent failures immediately after a major release. Application logs appear normal, but database connections and infrastructure resources are approaching their limits. As the senior .NET developer, how would you isolate the bottleneck, stabilise production, and determine whether the issue is architectural, application-level, or infrastructure-related?

sections.content: Treat the timing as a strong lead, not proof of causation. Establish an incident owner, assess user impact and compare the new release against healthy instances or the preceding version. Preserve traces and deployment metadata while deciding whether a safe rollback or feature-flag disablement will rapidly reduce impact.

Database connection saturation may reflect longer queries, leaked readers, wider transactions, higher request fan-out or excessive parallelism. Infrastructure saturation may be the cause or a downstream symptom. Compare connection hold time, request arrival rate, queue length, dependency spans and thread stacks.

Classify the evidence: an application regression might add N+1 calls; an architectural issue might create synchronous fan-out that grows with tenants; an infrastructure issue might impose an unexpected connection or network limit. More than one can contribute.

After stabilization, reproduce under representative concurrency, implement the smallest durable correction and canary the change. Add a regression check and alerts on saturation and tail latency. A successful incident response restores service first and then explains the causal chain without attributing everything to the last deployment.

variants.wording: Q4. Multiple development teams are building .NET services using different architectural patterns, coding standards, authentication approaches, and observability practices. Delivery speed is increasing, but maintenance complexity and production incidents are also rising. How would you establish engineering consistency without creating excessive governance or slowing autonomous teams?

sections.content: Establish a small set of shared requirements at costly boundaries: authentication, tenant isolation, observability, API error contracts, deployment safety and dependency hygiene. Let teams choose internal patterns where those choices do not create cross-team risk.

Provide maintained templates, libraries and pipeline checks so the easiest path meets the standard. Use architecture decision records and lightweight reviews for high-impact exceptions rather than requiring a central committee for every change.

Measure incident rate, onboarding time and delivery friction, and revise standards from real feedback. A paved path with clear ownership is more effective than a large document nobody can apply. Exceptions should be visible, justified and periodically reviewed.

questions.title: Reducing cloud cost by thirty percent

variants.wording: Q5. Leadership wants to reduce cloud and infrastructure costs by 30%, while product teams expect continued growth in traffic, availability, and feature velocity. How would you identify optimisation opportunities across .NET application performance, database usage, caching, compute, and architecture without creating technical debt that compromises future scalability?

sections.content: Build a baseline by service, environment and business unit, including cost per request or transaction. Identify idle capacity, oversized compute, expensive queries, data transfer, storage retention and telemetry volume before proposing an across-the-board cut.

Prioritize low-risk waste removal and measured performance improvements. Rightsize after observing peaks, schedule nonproduction capacity, optimize database reads and indexes, apply appropriate storage tiers and review cache effectiveness. Commitments or reservations fit predictable demand, not uncertain capacity.

Model the impact on availability, recovery and engineering effort. Validate changes against SLOs and realistic growth, then track realized savings rather than list-price estimates. Present a staged path toward thirty percent with assumptions; do not guarantee that target if the evidence shows it would compromise required reliability.

variants.wording: 18. How would you improve the performance of an ASP.NET Core API taking 5–10 seconds per request?
22. Scenario: Your API suddenly becomes slow in production. How would you identify whether the bottleneck is .NET, database, Redis, network, or external APIs?
4. What strategies do you use to optimize application performance, troubleshoot bottlenecks, and improve system reliability in production environments?
Q1. Your ASP.NET Core Web API is slow in production. How would you investigate and improve its performance?

sections.content: Start with the affected endpoints, time window, traffic, error rate and P50/P95/P99 latency, segmented by instance, tenant and region. Compare a slow trace with a healthy trace to locate time in request queuing, application work, SQL, Redis, external APIs or network activity.

For SQL, separate execution from pool waits and blocking. For Redis, inspect latency, connection pressure and cache misses. For external calls, inspect DNS/TLS, retries and timeouts. Within .NET, examine ThreadPool queues, blocked stacks, lock contention, allocation and GC pauses. Average CPU and memory can look healthy while requests wait.

Stabilize with a targeted rollback, traffic control, feature disablement or bounded concurrency when evidence supports it. Then fix the actual cause and validate under realistic load. Record the baseline and improvement; adding instances or caching without finding the bottleneck can merely move or amplify the problem.

variants.wording: 21. How would you design an ASP.NET Core API to handle 10K+ concurrent requests?
Q9. Your API must handle thousands of requests per minute. What changes would you make to improve scalability?

sections.content: Clarify the target: requests per minute is throughput, while concurrent requests are in-flight work. At steady state, concurrency is approximately arrival rate multiplied by response time. Ten thousand open requests can represent very different load depending on how much work each performs.

Use asynchronous I/O end to end, keep application instances stateless and bound queues and dependency concurrency. Optimize database access, paginate responses, cache suitable reads and move long jobs to durable background processing. Protect the system with rate limits and admission control.

Load-test the complete path, including gateway, database, Redis and external quotas. Scale horizontally only when shared dependencies can support it. Track tail latency and error budgets at the target load, and test graceful degradation when the system exceeds capacity rather than relying on a benchmark of one trivial endpoint.

variants.wording: A .NET Core API normally responds in 500ms but suddenly takes 8–10 seconds. There are no deployment changes, and DB, CPU, and memory look normal. How would you troubleshoot it?

sections.content: This expands and corrects the troubleshooting answer you supplied. First locate the extra time rather than assuming code or database failure. Check request rate, errors and latency percentiles for the same time window and segment by endpoint, instance, tenant and payload.

P50 of 500 ms means the median is 500 ms. P95 of 2 seconds means approximately 95 percent finish within 2 seconds, while P99 of 10 seconds marks the threshold near the slowest one percent. A high P99 with a healthy median indicates tail latency, but does not prove that only one percent of requests is affected; the full distribution matters.

Compare healthy and slow distributed traces, then follow the correlation ID through logs. Look for hidden retries, dependency timeouts, DNS/TLS delay, connection-pool waits, cache misses, locks and ThreadPool starvation. Normal aggregate CPU and database metrics do not exclude per-query blocking or a single unhealthy instance.

Without a deployment, investigate traffic/data shifts, secret rotation, DNS changes, certificate expiry, scheduled jobs, quota exhaustion and dependency incidents. Capture evidence before restarting. Apply a targeted mitigation, reproduce with representative conditions and verify the full latency distribution afterward.

variants.wording: 8. Describe a challenging production issue or system failure you resolved. What was your troubleshooting and root-cause analysis approach?
